articles.title: Reajuste do Bolsa Família é aposta de Lula para mudar foco da eleição após crise no STF | G1
articles.body:
O reajuste do Bolsa Família vinha sendo defendido havia algumas semanas por alas do Ministério da Fazenda como forma de conter o mau humor do eleitor com a economia. O martelo, no entanto, só foi batido depois da crise no Supremo Tribunal Federal. Dentro da campanha do presidente Lula à reeleição, a percepção é de que o movimento tira a disputa política da arena do Supremo, desfavorável a Lula.

A participação ativa do ministro Flávio Dino para postergar a abertura de investigação contra o ministro Alexandre de Moraes dificultou a narrativa de Lula de que "todos devem ser investigados".

Dino é, de todos, o ministro do Supremo mais associado ao presidente. Foi uma das caras do governo em seu primeiro biênio, com estilo combativo à frente do Ministério da Justiça, e com participação importante no pós 8 de janeiro.

O reajuste do Bolsa Família a 17 dias do primeiro turno suscita críticas. Mas, a avaliação da campanha é de que elas não fogem dos contrapontos tradicionalmente feitos à gestão do PT. Com ou sem o aumento, o cálculo é de que o governo já é lido como pouco preocupado com o fiscal.

Presidente Lula — Foto: Foto: Ricardo Stuckert.

Mais de 19 milhões de famílias recebem o Bolsa Família. A medida impacta quase 50 milhões de pessoas, cerca de um quarto da população brasileira. As últimas pesquisas têm mostrado uma insatisfação do eleitor com a economia, apesar de bons resultados dos indicadores, como baixa inflação e baixa taxa de desemprego.

A leitura no entorno de Lula é que, além de mudar a pauta da opinião pública, o reajuste funciona como um xeque na campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro: se criticar ou agir contra, ele corre o risco de perder votos.

Desde o início do dia, a coordenação da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro tem descartado agir contra medida que beneificia tanta gente.

O senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), coordenador da campanha, disse à GloboNews: "Não estão preocupados com o que vai acontecer no país adiante. Irresponsabilidade fiscal é a tônica deste governo. E na hora que isso acontece vem as consequências, como os juros estratosféricos. Vamos mostrar isso na campanha".

Mas, o processo foi extinto po André Mendonça por Trovão não ser um agente qualificado para propor esse tipo de ação. A medida foi vista como individual do parlamentar, mas gerou um passivo para a campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro.

Nos últimos dias, a campanha do presidente Lula começou a tentar mudar o tom da pauta.

Descontente com o controle da narrativa que Flávio Bolsonaro passou a ter com a crise no Supremo, articuladores do PT começaram a lembrar das crises do governo de Jair Bolsonaro e voltaram a atacar Donald Trump depois da inclusão de críticas ao Brasil no combate ao tráfico de drogas.

articles.title: LEE CARTER: The Fed finally raised rates. The real danger now for the GOP is what happens next
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates as inflation remains elevated, leaving consumers caught between higher borrowing costs and rising prices.
articles.body: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates Wednesday for the first time since 2023. There will be much discussion about what this means for the economy. There should be. But there is another question, less technical and perhaps more important as we approach the midterms. What does it mean to the people living in the economy? FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS The Fed sees an economy strong enough to withstand higher rates. Growth is solid. Consumers are still spending. Businesses are investing. The labor market is holding up. These are good things. And yet there is something strange about the word economists keep using to describe the American consumer. Resilient. Americans have certainly been that. They have absorbed years of higher prices. They have adjusted household budgets. They have postponed purchases. They have watched mortgage rates make houses they once could afford suddenly unaffordable. They have put more on credit cards and paid more interest for the privilege. US ECONOMY NOTCHES REMARKABLE NEW RECORD, SPARKING CHEERS: ‘GOOD JOB EVERYONE’ And they have kept going. But perhaps we’re asking too much of the word "resilient." A family can be resilient because it is thriving. It can also be resilient because it has no choice. A consumer can keep spending while putting more on a credit card. A small business can keep its doors open while canceling the expansion it hoped to finance. The spreadsheet calls that resilience. The voter may call it exhaustion. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: VOTERS SAY THEY’RE IN ECONOMIC PAIN, BUT WILL DEMOCRATS GAIN? There comes a point when people don’t want to hear that they’re weathering the storm remarkably well. They want the storm to end. That is the part of Wednesday’s decision Washington should be thinking about. The Federal Reserve raised rates because inflation remains too high. Higher interest rates are meant to slow demand. Borrowing becomes more expensive. People spend less. Businesses invest less. The economy cools and, eventually, inflation should cool with it. This is sound economic theory. It is also someone’s life. A small-business owner who was thinking about expanding now looks again at the cost of the loan. A young couple thinking about buying their first home runs the mortgage calculation one more time. A family that hasn’t paid off its credit card watches another month’s interest accumulate. None of them thinks: Monetary policy is working. They think: This is getting harder. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT And there is another complication. Some of today’s inflation pressure isn’t simply a story of Americans buying too much. Energy prices have surged amid geopolitical turmoil. Tariffs have added pressure to some goods prices. Supply matters, too. The Fed has a powerful tool for suppressing demand. It does not have a tool for producing oil. That distinction becomes important when the cure for higher prices is making money itself more expensive. Economist Mitch Roschelle put the larger dilemma this way: Monetary policy can suppress demand, but it cannot manufacture supply. The policies Washington says will eventually increase supply may take years to bear fruit. Voters aren’t living years from now. They’re voting this November, after the Federal Reserve has just delivered an unmistakable message: Inflation is still a problem. That leaves the consumer caught in the middle. The policies that might increase supply take time. The interest-rate hike designed to suppress demand does not. Its effects begin showing up in the cost of money now. And that may be the essential disconnect of this economy. FOX NEWS POLL: 'RESILIENT DISCONTENT' DEFINES THE US MOOD AT 250TH ANNIVERSARY Washington lives in the eventually. Consumers live in the now. Washington can debate whether today’s inflation began with pandemic spending, the Inflation Reduction Act, tariffs, oil prices, the war in the Middle East, consumer demand or some complicated combination of all of them. Voters don’t have to settle that argument. They know what a gallon of gas costs. THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH They know what they spent at the grocery store last Saturday. They know whether their credit-card balance is bigger than it was a year ago. They know whether the house they hoped to buy still feels possible. And they know whether they feel as if they are getting ahead or falling behind. That is why economic statistics and economic sentiment can tell such different stories. The statistics measure the economy. People measure their lives. There is, inevitably, a political dimension to all of this. IT’S NOT THE ECONOMY, STUPID. AMERICANS VOTE BASED ON THEIR PERSONAL ECONOMY President Trump has repeatedly called for lower interest rates. On Wednesday, the independent Federal Reserve looked at the economy and concluded that rates needed to go higher. Democrats will point to that decision as evidence that inflation remains a problem on Trump’s watch. Republicans will point to energy prices, geopolitical turmoil and other forces beyond the president’s control. Both arguments will be made loudly. But voters may hear something simpler. The president has said prices are coming under control. The Federal Reserve just said inflation remains elevated and raised interest rates to fight it. That doesn’t tell us who caused inflation. It tells us inflation isn’t over. And politically, that may be the more important distinction. Because Washington thinks about causation. People think about experience. GEN Z IS WORKING HARD, BUT THE ECONOMY IS PUTTING THE AMERICAN DREAM OUT OF REACH FOR MANY There is an echo here of the 1970s, although history is never as neat as politicians would like it to be. Then, too, oil shocks collided with an inflation problem already underway. Paul Volcker ultimately broke entrenched inflation with extraordinarily aggressive monetary tightening, at enormous economic cost. We are not living through the 1970s again. But history sometimes asks familiar questions. What happens when part of your inflation problem comes from things monetary policy cannot fix? And what happens when the cure lands on people who already feel they have been taking the medicine for years? That is why Wednesday’s Fed decision matters beyond the markets. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Politicians will argue about causation. Economists will allocate responsibility. Voters get to ask two considerably simpler questions: How am I doing? And: Who’s in charge? The Fed thinks the economy can take the medicine. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The question for November is how Americans feel after swallowing it.

articles.title: ‘Unprecedented’: Judges reveal behind-the-scenes coordination on Trump immigration cases
articles.summary: Minnesota federal judges coordinated via email threads and templates to handle habeas petitions during Operation Metro Surge, raising judicial ethics questions.
articles.body: Federal judges in Minnesota tasked with deciding a flood of habeas petitions challenging the detention of immigrants swept up during President Donald Trump's Operation Metro Surge weren't working entirely on their own — behind the scenes, they were regularly consulting one another through running email threads and developing tools to quickly handle recurring legal questions. The behind-the-scenes coordination among Minnesota's federal bench, revealed in a New York Times report Thursday, included regular meetings, running email threads, an informal spreadsheet created by court clerks showing which judges to turn to with particular legal questions and templates some judges developed to quickly issue orders when similar detention disputes repeatedly came before the court. The disclosures are fueling questions over whether the judges were colluding on separate cases involving the same Trump administration immigration policies, or simply sharing expertise to manage an extraordinary caseload. FEDERAL JUDGE TIES ICE AGENTS' HANDS WITH RULING ON WARRANTLESS SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ARRESTS "The idea of a running email chain involving a variety of cases — it strikes me as very weird and frankly unprecedented," Robert Luther III, a professor at George Mason University's Antonin Scalia Law School whose work includes federal courts and judicial ethics, told Fox News Digital. Federal judges can and routinely do consult colleagues, Luther said, particularly about procedural or evidentiary questions. But each judge is ultimately responsible for independently deciding the cases assigned to them — a distinction Luther said makes the coordination significant. The disclosures have also drawn criticism from the Trump administration on two fronts. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) General Counsel James Percival accused the former chief judge who led the district during Metro Surge of "essentially conspiring with his judicial colleagues" to thwart federal immigration enforcement. The Justice Department (DOJ), meanwhile, questioned the decision by sitting judges to give extensive on-the-record interviews about their experience with the administration's immigration operation. Seven of the district's judges spoke to the Times for Thursday's report, including former Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz, who sat for a 90-minute interview about the court's experience during Metro Surge. Schiltz declined to discuss ongoing cases, according to the Times, but described what happened in Minnesota's federal court as having "created a grave threat to the rule of law." "It is remarkable that sitting federal judges are giving on-the-record interviews attacking this Administration's policies rather than ruling from the bench," a Justice Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "If judges followed the law in adjudicating cases, there wouldn't be an 'overwhelming' habeas caseload. Judges who have made public comments on pending or related matters should consider whether recusal is warranted going forward." OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’ But Chief Judge Eric Tostrud, who was himself among the Minnesota judges interviewed by the Times, rejected suggestions that the coordination described in the report compromised individual decision-making. He told Fox News Digital that every member of the bench independently decided the merits of each petition assigned to them, while pointing to an extraordinary surge in litigation — from 12 alien-detainee habeas petitions during all of 2024 to 1,427 through August of this year — and noting that many involved similar or identical, often novel, legal questions. "The bottom line is that each of us made an independent decision with respect to the merits of each and every petition we were assigned," Tostrud told Fox News Digital. Tostrud stressed that the judges did not uniformly reach the same conclusions, saying that while some reached the same result on certain legal questions, they "reached different outcomes regarding other legal questions." He said the judges' ability to communicate helped them resolve the cases quickly and thoughtfully, regardless of whether individual petitions were granted. What exactly the judges were sharing behind the scenes, however, remains unclear. Tostrud declined to disclose the contents of the court's internal working materials, saying documents created by judges and court staff "are not public." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY That distinction could be significant, according to Luther, who said administrative templates are commonplace in federal courts, but drew a line between those and templates touching the substance of a case. "Templates that deal with administrative matters strike me as entirely appropriate and commonplace in federal courts," Luther said. "Templates for substantive matters — that seems like something altogether different." The coordination unfolded amid a broader clash between Minnesota's federal bench and the Trump administration over Operation Metro Surge. The dispute came as immigration litigation inundated the district. During the first three months of 2026, Minnesota's federal court received 1,116 habeas petitions, compared with just two during the same period the previous year, according to the Times. Court staff worked 16-hour days, seven days a week, to process the incoming cases. Patrick Schiltz, who served as the district's chief judge during Metro Surge before taking senior status — a form of semi-retirement — this summer, emerged as a prominent judicial critic of the administration's handling of the operation. In a Jan. 28 order, Schiltz accused ICE of violating nearly 100 court orders during that month and warned that "ICE is not a law unto itself." OBAMA JUDGE'S PECULIAR TRUMP REBUKE IGNITES FURY OVER 'UNPROFESSIONAL' LANGUAGE: 'EMBARRASSMENT' The cases cited in Schiltz's January list of alleged violations have largely concluded, according to the Times, which reported that the administration ultimately corrected the issues flagged by the court in many of them. DOJ said its review of the cases found that in the "large majority" of them, detainees were released on time and no violation occurred, while in most of the remaining cases the department said it ultimately did what the court ordered despite missing an additional deadline. MASSACHUSETTS' HIGHEST COURT PUBLICLY REPRIMANDS JUDGE ACCUSED OF ENABLING IMMIGRANT TO ESCAPE ICE Federal judicial ethics rules generally prohibit judges from publicly commenting on the merits of pending or impending cases, but permit judges to explain court procedures and engage in broader speaking and teaching about the law, legal system and administration of justice. The DOJ argued that judges who publicly commented on pending or related matters should consider whether recusal is warranted. The Times reported, however, that Schiltz declined to discuss ongoing cases, while Judge Nancy Brasel, a Trump appointee who also participated in the interviews, defended judges' ability to speak publicly about judicial independence. "We are allowed to speak out about judicial independence," Brasel told the Times. "And so we should, in order to keep it." Luther, however, took a different view of the judges' decision to participate in the interviews. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Judges should be speaking through their judicial orders, not through their surrogates at The New York Times," he told Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Republicans wanted to run against Mamdani. They're running against Hochul instead.
articles.summary: The moderate governor has been targeted by GOP campaigns as the symbol of a deep blue state’s policies — and even her fellow Democrats are keeping her at arm...
articles.body:
NEW YORK — Not too long ago, Republicans were salivating at the thought of using New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as a far-left boogeyman. Instead, moderate Gov. Kathy Hochul has emerged as the GOP's go-to foil.

As Hochul runs for a second term, Republicans are hoping her middling popularity will be a drag on Democrats in competitive down-ballot races. Some Democratic candidates, meanwhile, are keeping her at arm's length — a sign they recognize the downside of appearing with a governor often linked to Albany's reputation for high taxes and lax criminal justice laws.

"There's not a Democrat in the party in a swing district who wants to be near her," said a state Democratic official, granted anonymity to speak candidly. "Her numbers aren't as bad as four years ago, but they're certainly not good."

The current state of play is one neither party fully planned for. Mamdani, a 34-year-old democratic socialist who campaigned on freezing rents and taxing the rich, was supposed to be the Democrat who repelled suburban and upstate voters. Hochul has spent four years trying to be the Democrat who repels no one. Yet outside the city, the socialist is a curiosity and the governor a grievance.

After less than a year in office, Mamdani has amassed high favorability ratings in New York City and a positive perception nationally , while the suburbs ringing the city remain cooler on him. Hochul is being invoked far more broadly. Since casting Mamdani as a socialist neophyte carries less weight farther outside the city, Republicans have fixed their sights more squarely on her as the prime personification of the state's leftward lurch.

New York, home to a handful of swing districts expected to determine control of the House, remains a high priority for both parties. And the top-of-ticket race between Hochul and Republican nominee Bruce Blakeman stands to impact voter turnout in races beyond their own.

"Outside of the New York City media market, Mamdani doesn't have the same impact," said Marc Molinaro, a former House lawmaker and ex-Trump administration official who's now running for the state Assembly. "Most people further north just don't have a relationship with the city. They may not love the city, they may not have an attachment to the city, but who do they see? They see the governor."

On suburban Long Island, former state Assemblymember Mike LiPetri used his first television advertisement of the general election to decry "career politicians like Kathy Hochul and Tom Suozzi who sold us out and left us behind." The opening screed in Rep. Nick LaLota's TV spot is that "Kathy Hochul's taxes are the worst in the nation." And GOP candidate Anthony Constantino, running to succeed Rep. Elise Stefanik in a blood red upstate district, has accused his Democratic foe Blake Gendebien of being "beaten into submission" by the governor after he pulled a TV ad pledging to stand up to her .

In a statement, Hochul spokesperson Ryan Radulovacki said: "No amount of GOP spin changes the fact that New York Republicans gutted Medicaid, ripped food assistance from families and kids, and enabled Donald Trump, a historically unpopular president, as he tried to defund the NYPD and raised costs on everything from gas to groceries – while Governor Hochul put money back in New Yorkers' pockets, passed free school meals, and stood up to Trump at every turn. Voters across this state see all of that, and they're going to send Republicans a message in less than 50 days."

Republicans are facing a tough midterm election with an unpopular president in the White House. They are trying to weather a political dynamic featuring widespread voter angst over costs, with high interest rates and spiking gas prices emerging as resonant plotlines in the Empire State. Losses in purplish and even red areas of New York would go a long way to costing Republicans the House.

Making Hochul the face of a Democratic Party framed around taxes and crime is meant to counter an otherwise bleak Republican environment and President Donald Trump's unpopularity here.

But Democrats are casting doubt on how effective such messaging will be — especially compared to the GOP candidates' association with Trump.

"I don't think it's anywhere near as potent as the president of the United States," said consultant David Carlucci. "It is just a lash out as really one of the few options they have in terms of just playing the blame game."

Meanwhile, Democrats are trying to thread a delicate needle as the governor seeks a second full term. Some are attempting to separate themselves from Hochul — a dance made all the more awkward as she marshals the resources of the New York Democratic Committee to aid down-ballot candidates.

In the North Country, Gendebien told supporters recently that Hochul is "unpopular" and "underwater" in the district he's seeking to represent. According to a recording of a Sept. 3 town hall that was obtained by POLITICO , he also acknowledged that he didn't know why.

Even in races where a high-profile surrogate could be a welcome boost to a relative unknown, the desire for the governor to stump isn't necessarily strong. When asked if Hochul would be helpful on the trail for him, Mike DeCillis, a long shot Democrat challenging Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, replied: "Probably not."

The district, a red-leaning seat that covers all of Staten Island and part of Brooklyn, is a "fickle pickle," he said. "It's not because of any specific policy. It's the person they have been kind of trained and told that this is the person they shouldn't like at all costs."

Hochul's zealous push for House Democrats — a years-long project launched after former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi blamed her weak showing in 2022 for losing down-ballot races — has further raised the stakes in a race that she's largely expected to win. In 2022, she won by only 6 points.

"We're going to be the state that sends Hakeem Jeffries to the speaker's office," Hochul said in an interview on NY1 , highlighting her investment into the state party. She expressed confidence in flipping districts held by Rep. Mike Lawler, Lalota and Stefanik, and holding those represented by Suozzi and Reps. Laura Gillen, Josh Riley, Pat Ryan and John Mannion.

It's unclear where exactly Hochul will stump for down-ballot candidates in the closing stretch of the election, though an aide said she will be supporting candidates up and down the ballot.

Republicans viewed Mamdani, of all people, to be their primary weapon in the suburbs and upstate, where voters tend to be moderate and more willing to back a Republican. But the mayor, who was viewed favorably by 69% of New York City voters in an August Siena Research Institute poll , has not been the beat-up toy many GOP candidates expected.

New York City mayors, who often bring left-leaning agendas into office, are typically viewed as easy targets for Republicans, especially in rural and suburban House districts. That strategy hasn't always been effective, in part, because few voters outside the five boroughs consider the city's mayor to be especially relevant.

"I've been asked many times, like, where does upstate and downstate start?" Republican state Sen. Peter Oberacker, who's challenging Democratic Rep. Josh Riley, said in an interview last month. "You could almost determine where that line is by the concern about Mamdani. … In the more northern reaches of our district, it's definitely a topic of discussion and concern. But as you come farther downstate, it gets a bit more intense."

When asked whether the governor or mayor comes up more in discussions with voters, he said the former — and pointed to Hochul allocating $4 billion to help the city's budget gap. "They feel this way that they're not getting represented," he said.

Riley doesn't view Hochul as much of an issue. He touted her work tackling a dearth of affordable child care. "I'm eager to continue working on that with her," he said in a statement.

In a state where Democrats hold all levers of power, Hochul is an obvious focal point for Republicans — the embodiment of a deep blue state's policies on taxes, crime and regulations that drive up utility bills.

She's tried to reverse that perception. She's backed measures to scale back a controversial cashless bail law and touted middle-income tax cuts and rebate checks. And she's embraced popular policies like expanding no-cost child care, banning cellphones in schools and a moratorium on data center construction.

But those policies are more popular than the governor herself.

The Siena survey found 49% of voters hold an unfavorable view of Hochul, with only 46% reporting a favorable opinion. Yet most voters back her efforts to curb Trump's aggressive deportation campaign and New York's data center construction pause, which Hochul rolled out this summer. The same poll found Hochul leading Blakeman by 10 points, with the largest chunk of her support coming from the city. She trailed Blakeman in the suburbs by 8 points, and they were nearly tied upstate.

Trump is even more unpopular with New York voters: Only 38% have a favorable view of him. He was slightly above water in the suburbs, but viewed unfavorably upstate and in NYC.

Despite those numbers, some Democratic candidates may not have much of a choice but to accept Hochul's help.

The governor is using the state Democratic Committee this year to aid down-ballot candidates, opening field offices and providing political infrastructure to support those running in crucial races. This coordinated campaign is a stark departure from prior years when the state party functioned solely as an arm of the governor's political operation.

The shift began in 2024 and is carrying over into this election year, as Democrats try to hold several seats on Long Island and in the Hudson Valley.

"She absolutely delivered in 2024 on this in a huge way," said Rep. Pat Ryan, whose seat is not seen as competitive as it was two years ago. "She campaigned a bunch of times for me in that race and across the Hudson Valley and I dramatically outperformed in large part because of a lot of the things that she did. That's only grown stronger now."

New York Democrats must win without relying solely on Hochul's coattails to carry them, though.

Distance themselves too far from the governor, and candidates run the risk of undermining the head of their party set on returning to Albany with a clear mandate for the next four years. Running too close with Hochul opens up swing seat candidates to Republican attacks that they're the lackeys of a chief executive with so-so polling.

Ryan's neighboring House member, Lawler, is viewed as one of the most vulnerable Republicans in the country. Earlier this year, he rallied with Trump — not the most popular figure in the district — and said he'd welcome Hochul to campaign for his Democratic opponent Cait Conley "any day of the week."

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly carried the district, as Lawler won reelection.

With that past as prologue in mind, it remains unclear if Conley will appear with Hochul on the trail. But she's bringing in other reinforcements. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a potential 2028 presidential contender, campaigned with her in the district this week.

Conley has said outright that she does not want to campaign with Mamdani — a calculus that speaks to the independent-minded voters she needs to get on her side. Republicans have sought to tie them together in an attempt to portray her as too far to the left.

Lawler has repeatedly invoked both Mamdani and Hochul on the trail. At times, he's trained more of his ire at the governor than his actual opponent.

"Their numbers are very similar in the district, and for different reasons and in different ways, they are equally as offensive to most voters in the district," Lawler said of Hochul and Mamdani.

Still, Hochul's allies believe it's an error for Democratic candidates to disassociate themselves from the de facto head of the party. If she wins in November, she'll continue to wield substantial power.

"I've never felt that running away from the head of your ticket is a winning strategy for any party in any year," New York Democratic Party Chair Jay Jacobs said. "You make a mistake by distancing yourself from her where she can be helpful."

articles.title: Born in Cairo, raised in Texas: Meet Dina Powell McCormick, the executive Mark Zuckerberg asked to trade her Meta board seat for a job
articles.summary: Tech News News: Mark Zuckerberg took a walk around Koolau Ranch, his compound in Kauai, with one of his newest board members last December and made her an unusual off.
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg took a walk around Koolau Ranch, his compound in Kauai, with one of his newest board members last December and made her an unusual offer. Give up the seat, he said, and come work inside the company instead. He told Dina Powell McCormick, who had joined the Meta board only eight months earlier, that the $1.7 trillion company was betting its future on artificial intelligence, that it would have to raise a tremendous amount of outside capital to do it, and that he needed an adviser who could smooth the way with financial institutions and governments alike.It would be the most important job she would ever have, he told her. She resigned from the board about a week later. In January she came back as president, vice chairman and co-leader of Meta Compute, the division building and monetising the infrastructure behind the AI push. Nine months in, a Bloomberg report drawing on interviews with more than a dozen Meta insiders, outside executives and government officials describes her as the person Zuckerberg and his top deputies hand the company's thorniest problems.That remit has stretched well past compute deals. She has weighed in on Meta's biggest legal and reputational fights, including a settlement of up to $18 billion with state attorneys general over children's safety on Instagram and Facebook, and on the backlash to AI itself. She has appeared for Meta at Davos, travelled to China with President Donald Trump and an entourage of Silicon Valley's best-known names, and met King Charles III. Zuckerberg says it became clear "she could play a bigger role in Meta's next chapter".A state senate internship in Texas led her to Goldman Sachs and then the White HouseShe was born Dina Habib in Cairo, Egypt and moved to Texas at the age of four, after her parents decided the United States offered their daughter better odds. She studied at the University of Texas at Austin, started with an internship in the state senate, and worked her way through Republican politics to become assistant secretary of state for educational and cultural affairs under Condoleezza Rice.In 2007 she joined Goldman Sachs, stayed 16 years, made partner and built programmes such as 10,000 Small Businesses and 10,000 Women. She returned to Washington in 2017 as deputy national security adviser for strategy, focused on West Asia, and was the only woman at the table when Trump met Saudi Arabia's King Salman. She left government in 2018, went back to Goldman, then to merchant bank BDT & MSD Partners. Her husband, David McCormick, is a Republican senator from Pennsylvania. Between them they have six daughters.Meta's AI spending is rising fast and someone has to sell itThe timing explains the hire. Meta has raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to between $125 billion and $145 billion, up from $115 billion to $135 billion, and the stock fell 9% after that disclosure. The company also plans to cut 10% of its workforce, roughly 8,000 jobs, while fighting the FTC's appeal in the Instagram and WhatsApp antitrust case and a youth-addiction verdict over social media design.Her pitch leans away from data centres and towards users. Meta's AI tools, she says, are meant to "empower people like small-business owners, welders, the fiber technicians, creators". She has also pushed the point that women are adopting AI more slowly than men, and that Meta should fix it.Zuckerberg, 42, stays in Menlo Park with the researchers. Powell McCormick, 53, handles everyone else.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Democrat leads Marshall in tight Kansas Senate race: Poll
articles.summary: Democrat Adam Hamilton narrowly leads Republican Gov. Roger Marshall in a tight race for Senate in red Kansas, according to new polling. Another 4 percent chose Libertarian candidate David Graham, and 8 percent were…
articles.body:
Democrat Adam Hamilton narrowly leads Republican Gov. Roger Marshall in a tight race for Senate in red Kansas, according to new polling.

A new The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey found Hamilton ahead by 2 percentage points, with 45 percent to Marshall’s 43 percent. Another 4 percent chose Libertarian candidate David Graham, and 8 percent were undecided.

“This poll finds Democrats with their best chance to win their first Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, in part driven by Democrat Hamilton’s appeal to independent voters, leading by 15 points,” said Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling.

Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race toward Democrats last month, from “solid” to “likely” Republican, citing Hamilton’s primary win as a promising sign for Democrats hoping to break “a nearly century-long Senate losing streak” in Kansas. Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) also considers the race likely Republican.

Hamilton, senior pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, is campaigning to become the first Democrat to win a Sunflower State Senate race since former Sen. George McGill in 1932. Marshall is vying for a second term after winning the seat by double-digits in 2020.

Former Republican Gov. Bill Graves (Kansas) backed Hamilton this week, saying the country is “facing increasing partisan gridlock and division” and that it’s “time Kansas does something different.”

Graham’s third-party candidacy “shakes up the Senate race in a way we do not see in the governor’s contest,” Kimball added, noting that the Libertarian’s supporters “break heavily” for the Republican contender in the governor’s race to replace term-limited Gov. Laura Kelly (D).

Democrat Cindy Holscher, a state senator backed by Kelly for the governor’s mansion, trailed behind Republican Ty Masterson, the state Senate president backed by President Trump, with 44 percent to Masterson’s 51 percent. Another 6 percent were undecided.

“Independents are splitting their ticket: in the race for Governor, they break for Masterson by two points, 47 percent to 45 percent,” Kimball noted.

Cook Political Report and DDHQ both consider the governor’s race to lean Republican.

In a potential signal of Democratic momentum in Kansas, which voted for Trump in each of his three elections, Vice President Vance stopped by and touted Kansas Republicans this week.

Friday’s survey was conducted Sept. 15-16 among 750 likely voters and had a credibility interval, similar to a poll’s margin of error, of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points.

articles.title: GOP faces reality check as they try to hold onto House majority
articles.summary: Republicans are heading into the final stretch of the midterm race recognizing a blunt message: Voters are frustrated, and acknowledging those frustrations might be key to keeping them in the GOP column. Republicans have been increasingly framing the election as a choice between “common sense” versus “communist crazy” — arguing that democratic socialist and progressive…
articles.body:
Republicans are heading into the final stretch of the midterm race recognizing a blunt message: Voters are frustrated, and acknowledging those frustrations might be key to keeping them in the GOP column.

Republicans have been increasingly framing the election as a choice between “common sense” versus “communist crazy” — arguing that democratic socialist and progressive candidates would make life worse for the American people.

At the same time, the party is confronting the limits of running on its record in Washington at a moment when gas prices, grocery costs, a chaotic immigration crackdown and the war with Iran have given voters fresh reasons to question the direction of the country and put Republicans on the defensive.

Vice President Vance underscored that reality during a closed-door House Republican meeting Tuesday, urging lawmakers to level with voters rather than paper over their frustrations — and place the fault squarely on Democrats.

“Right now we have a country where people are frustrated. You got to level with them,” Vance said, according to audio obtained by The Hill. “You got to be honest about those frustrations, and you got to be honest about the ways in which the Democrats caused the problems that you guys have been very diligently fixing over the past 18 months.”

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent lawmakers home early on Wednesday, canceling votes on Thursday and scrapping the last two weeks of the September session. He argued that much of the legislative agenda has been stalled in the Senate and that lawmakers could spend the extra time on the campaign trail.

Still, the stakes are particularly high for Republicans in the lower chamber, who are defending a razor-thin majority heading into an election cycle where the president’s party historically faces defeat.

“This midterm is going to be a f—ing bloodbath,” Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), who is exiting Congress after losing the South Carolina GOP gubernatorial primary, told reporters Wednesday. “There’s a lot at stake. The Senate is at stake. The House is at stake. The future of our country is at stake. I would tell you that the midterms of 2026 are a precursor to 2028.”

Asked whether she thinks Republicans will win the midterms, Mace said, “No, I don’t.”

“I’m concerned about it. When the economy is the way that it is, when rates are up, when the price, the affordability, and the cost of living is up where it is traditionally, the majority goes the other direction in a midterm election,” Mace said.

An Economist/YouGov poll of 1,536 adults conducted between Aug. 21-24 found that only 28 percent of Americans were satisfied with the economy while 64 percent were dissatisfied. The poll showed that Democrats have a 7-point lead over Republicans on the question of which party does a better job on economic issues.

It also found that 39 percent of Americans said Democrats are stronger on the economy while 32 percent said Republicans are better at handling the issue.

And a recent New York Times/Siena poll conducted between Sept. 8-13 among 1,503 likely voters found that 50 percent trust Democrats to do a better job handling foreign wars, while 43 percent of voters trust Republicans more.

The war with Iran has spiked gas prices — a very visible and deeply felt economic marker. The national average for regular unleaded gas jumped from $4.31 to $4.43 in the span of four days this week, according to AAA . A year ago, the average was $3.20.

Meanwhile, the national average for diesel jumped 42 cents over the last week.

The concerns over the Iran issue were on full display this week, after seven Republicans joined Democrats in voting for a war powers resolution that would limit President Trump’s military actions in the country, an increase from the four who previously supported similar resolutions.

Republican Reps. Zach Nunn (Iowa) and Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa) — two of the new “yes” votes — are competing in seats rated toss-ups by the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report.

“I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” Miller-Meeks wrote on social media after the vote.

“The Iranian regime and its nuclear ambitions have been defanged. The President needs to present a plan to Congress and the American people for how this ends so we can focus on bringing our soldiers home and lowering prices,” she added.

Nunn echoed similar sentiments, arguing in a statement that Iowa “has already paid a devastating price, including two service members killed by an Iranian drone in Kuwait.”

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who earlier this week introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, predicted Wednesday that a lot of GOP incumbents will lose their race over the conflict.

“You know, maybe it’s not a thing that moves 20 percent of people, but it could move 5 or 10 percent and even if it’s not the war that they dislike so much, it’s the consequences of war, which is the price of diesel and gasoline, and so it’s a big issue. I mean, this was Donald Trump’s election to lose, and he’s doing everything he can to lose it,” Massie, who lost his GOP primary to a Trump-backed opponent in May, told reporters.

Some incumbents running in tight districts have tried to distance themselves from Trump and his policies, as they attempt to appeal to a broad electorate.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), for instance, accused Trump of going “too far” with some of his immigration enforcement efforts in a campaign advertisement released Thursday. Salazar’s district has one of the highest foreign-born populations of any House district.

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar, whose seat is rated as likely Republican by Cook Political Report, said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism.”

Republicans are pointing to their legislative accomplishments, including the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as evidence they are addressing many of the issues that Americans are impacted by most at home.

And they are asking voters to give them two more years to continue fixing what they accuse Democrats of breaking.

“Rome was not built in a day, and so I always find that actually leveling with the American people is very powerful. Saying we know that there’s a lot of work left to do,” Vance told Republicans this week. “We know that we got to keep on at it.”

“But the problem is the Democrats are not. They are the arsonists. They are the people who started the fire. So, when you’re trying to fix these problems, do you give Republicans another two years to continue to work and fix the problems we’ve been fixing, or we hand power back over to the very people who caused the problem to begin with. That message to me has done a lot more, and I’ve seen it in the polling than just going out there and pretending that everything is perfect,” the vice president continued.

Johnson echoed that message in a press conference Tuesday.

“Just less than two years ago, we had a country on the brink of ruin. We had criminals, and cartels had free reign over the border. You all remember that Americans of all ages were dying from fentanyl overdoses. Great scourge upon the country. Inflation soared over 9 percent under [former President] Joe Biden, a 40-year high … In 2024 the people said that’s enough. They wanted a change, so they elected and returned Donald J. Trump back to the White House, and they gave our party, the Republicans, control the House and Senate. In just 19 short months since that happened, we have turned the ship of state around,” he said.

“We have changed the course of the country. We put ourselves on that new path, and it is well underway,” the Speaker added.

articles.title: Iran live updates: US rejects UN report on possible war crimes in Minab school strike
articles.summary: Trump made the remarks during an interview with Axios published Thursday.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28, with massive joint U.S.-Israeli strikes targeting military, government and infrastructure sites.

Delegations from the U.S. and Iran entered negotiations in June aimed at a war-ending deal based on a memorandum of understanding signed by both countries.

Those talks broke down as the U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes, with the strategic Strait of Hormuz as the primary flashpoint. Trump then said in August that the U.S. would launch a "crushing economic operation" to force Tehran into submission.

The average price for a gallon of diesel was still hovering around a record-high of $6.43 as of Friday morning, according to the latest data published by GasBuddy. Oil prices, meanwhile, edged lower but remained above $100 a barrel. Brent crude oil prices, a benchmark for global trading, were around $103 per barrel as of Friday morning, down roughly 1.3%. WTI crude oil, used as the North American benchmark, was trading at around $102 per barrel down 0.4%. The nationwide average price for a gallon of regular gas was at $4.47 as of Friday, according to GasBuddy -- up $1.53 since the U.S. war with Iran started.

Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto confirmed on Friday that an Italian Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet was "hit" during a Thursday night attack on the King Fahad Air Base in southwestern Saudi Arabia. "An Italian F-2000 aircraft was hit, which was located inside the base in a remote area," Crosetto said in a statement posted to X by the Italian Defense Ministry, using the Italian air force's designation for the Typhoon. "There are no other damages to vehicles or infrastructure used by our personnel." The air base, Crosetto said, "has been the target of several attacks." Italian troops engaged in Operation Inherent Resolve -- the U.S.-led coalition campaign against ISIS -- are deployed at the facility, which is also known as the Taif air base. Crosetto did say who was responsible for the strike. The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have claimed multiple drone and ballistic missile attacks on the King Fahad Air Base in recent weeks.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Friday said that Seoul will not engage in the ongoing U.S.-Iran war, as the country weighs plans to contribute to future maritime security operations in the Strait of Hormuz. "Let it be clear. There will be no dispatch of troops that will lead to involvement in a conflict. There will be no engagement or involvement in war," Lee said in a televised press conference, as quoted by the Yonhap News Agency. "The principle of no engagement or involvement in war has been observed so far and will continue to be observed in the future," he added. South Korea has faced pressure from President Donald Trump to provide active support for U.S. military operations against Iran. Last month, Trump ordered the curtailment of planned joint U.S.-South Korean military drills, a decision he said was in part due to Seoul's refusal to join the conflict.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported that a tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" in the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Friday morning. The impact caused a fire onboard the vessel, which was later extinguished, the UKMTO said. All crew members were reported safe, the alert added.

The State Department is pushing back on a UN-commissioned report that found there is "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. committed war crimes in Iran, including during a strike on a primary school in Minab. "The Trump Administration formally withdrew from the UN Human Rights Council following the Council's consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric and antisemitism, all while it appeases repressive regimes, thus making a mockery of the very 'rights' it claims to protect," a State Department official said. "As such, we do not give credibility" to the findings of the report. The official continued: "The protection of civilians is of the utmost importance to the U.S. We refer to the Department of War with respect to specific questions on U.S. operations." In regards to Minab, the report—which relies on open source reporting—concluded the attack on the school "went beyond mere negligence." "Rather, the U.S. directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen," the report stated. The report also notes that investigators sent a request for information to the U.S. government, as well as requests for meetings, but that their requests went unanswered. The fact-finding mission also concluded that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity, saying the number of casualties caused by the regime's crackdown earlier this year could not be verified, but that it was likely "significantly higher" than figures reported by Iran's government (3,038 killed, 25,000 injured.) -ABC News' Shannon Kingston

President Donald Trump told Axios in an interview published Thursday that he has a "big decision" coming up on whether to "go in and annihilate" the Iranian regime. "I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me," Trump said, according to Axios. According to Axios, during the interview "Trump declined to say whether he'll decide on the path forward before or after the midterms." -ABC News' Michelle Stoddart

Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense Directorate announced on Thursday that shrapnel from a downed Houthi drone killed at least one person and injured two others in the Taif Governorate, in the southwestern Mecca Province. The shrapnel also caused "material damage to several buildings and vehicles," the directorate said in a statement posted to X. -ABC News' Othon Leyva

The State Department announced on Wednesday that it had extended sanctions denying visas to Palestinian Authority officials and members of the Palestinian Liberation Organization, saying that officials "have, once again, failed to live up to their commitments" required by U.S. law. "It is in our national interest to impose consequences and hold the PLO and PA accountable for glorifying terrorism," the State Department said in a press release. The move effectively bars a high-level Palestinian delegation -- including Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas -- from traveling to New York for the upcoming United Nations General Assembly high-level week. The measure does contain a carveout for personnel assigned to the PLO observer mission at the UN. -ABC News' Shannon K. Kingston

U.S. bases in the Middle East have suffered severe damage as a result of Iranian attacks, images and videos obtained by ABC News show, as the Pentagon surveys the costs of a war the U.S. began more than six months ago. The images, which were recently obtained by ABC News but capture moments in time across the conflict, show damage to buildings and an aircraft at three U.S. bases in Kuwait and a Saudi base that houses U.S. assets, some of which were evacuated amid the danger. A senior U.S. service member told ABC News that the damage to the facilities would take "decades" to repair.

President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday that he hopes that the U.S. is "toward the end of the war" with Iran. "Well, hopefully we're toward the end of the war," Trump said on the tarmac in North Carolina when asked by a reporter how he would describe what phase the war is in. "They want to make a deal. We'll see how that works out." When asked whether there are intermediaries in the negotiations with Iranians, Trump said, "We deal directly." -ABC News' Michelle Stoddart and Devin Garbitt

articles.title: Jasmine Crockett torched for honoring singer with notorious history of violence: 'Completely vile'
articles.summary: Jasmine Crockett entered Chris Brown into the congressional record, sparking fierce backlash over his felony assault conviction involving Rihanna.
articles.body: Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, who recently lost her Senate bid, is facing online backlash after she honored music artist Chris Brown by entering him into the congressional record this past weekend. "Now, y’all know, I tend to get in trouble every once in a while. I’m a make this real quick. I need to know who run it! So is Dallas in the building?" Crockett said as she took the stage alongside Brown on Saturday evening. "Let’s give it up for Chris Brown," she added to applause from the audience. The moment drew scrutiny from viewers online, raising questions about Crockett’s status as a lawmaker and whether it should be used to celebrate Brown, someone with a history of domestic violence. AMERICA OWES BLACK WOMEN 'EVERYTHING,' REP JASMINE CROCKETT RANTS OVER JULY 4 WEEKEND Among other instances of misconduct, Brown pleaded guilty in 2009 to felony assault after he attacked his then-girlfriend and famous singer, Rihanna. Many images of her injuries were made public, sparking intense condemnation from the music industry. His violence, however, wouldn’t stop there. He was involved in a 2013 altercation with Frank Ocean, another singer, and pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor assault charge that same year. In 2017, another ex-girlfriend was granted a domestic violence restraining order against him after she alleged physical abuse. Most recently, Brown pleaded guilty to charges of striking producer Abe Diaw twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in July 2023. He is expected to receive a sentence in October for a separate charge for affray, a criminal charge in English law for unlawfully threatening violence against another person. Andrew Kerr, an investigative reporter with the Washington Free Beacon, quickly noted Brown’s past in a post to X after news of Crockett’s tribute began to spread online. "Kamala Harris-endorsed Rep. Jasmine Crockett uses her congressional authority to honor Chris Brown, the rapper best known for beating ever-living s--- out of Rihanna in 2009," Kerr wrote. Shannon Watts, a Democratic activist and political commentator, also pointed out Brown’s storied past. WATCH: HEARING TURMOIL AS JASMINE CROCKETT UNLOADS ON MLK'S NIECE IN WILD RACIALLY-CHARGED RANT "Chris Brown pled guilty to felony assault after brutally attacking Rihanna. Another ex, Karrueche Tran, later obtained a five-year restraining order after testifying that he abused and threatened her. He has also faced multiple allegations of violence and sexual assault against other women," Watts wrote. Crockett’s member statement, a form of recognition that lawmakers can have entered into the congressional record without any vote, recognizes "the artistry of Chris Brown and Usher Raymond." On stage on Saturday, Crockett framed her member statement as a way to recognize two key artists who had helped shape contemporary R&B and pop music, especially for the Black community. "I know it’s almost Sunday, so I wanna be clear. Weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning. And right now, we are experiencing Black joy to the highest level, and I wanted to make sure we document that in the Congressional Record," Crockett said. But Democratic strategist Ameshia Cross believes that the moment was a political miscalculation, coming across as ignorant of the challenges in the Black community. "Chris Brown has a problem, and several folks beyond Rihanna have met his violent rage. It’s well-documented. This was a ridiculous move by Crockett," she wrote on X. articles.title: Possible measles exposure reported at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia
articles.summary: The notice comes after the state reported two recent measles-related deaths, bringing its total this year to four.
articles.body:
PHILADELPHIA ( WPHL ) – Philadelphia health officials are warning about a possible measles exposure at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The possible exposure at CHOP potentially took place on Friday, Sept. 11, at 3401 Civic Center Boulevard, officials said in an announcement Thursday night.

Here are the locations and times of the possible exposure:

CHOP NICU West Family Lounge: 9:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m.

CHOP Main Cafeteria: 12:05 p.m. to 2:45 p.m.

“CHOP, the Pennsylvania Department of Health, and PDPH are working closely to ensure infants in the NICU receive a preventative antibody product to prevent or lessen severe disease and to take steps to prevent the further spread of measles,” officials said in the announcement. “PDPH is encouraging people who were exposed to check their vaccination status and watch for symptoms.”

The incident comes after the state reported two recent measles-related deaths , bringing the total this year to four.

“We encourage people to get vaccinated not only to protect themselves, but to protect those who cannot get vaccinated,” said Health Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson. “This is why it is imperative that everyone who is eligible gets up to date on the vaccines they need so we can protect our most vulnerable.”

Raval-Nelson went on to say that officials “do not believe that these exposures constitute a broad risk to Philadelphians, since the vast majority of us are fully protected due to our being vaccinated,” but urged those without protection to get their vaccinations “as soon as possible.”

“Remember, this is not just about protecting yourself, it’s about protecting our most vulnerable Philadelphians.”

Measles is highly contagious. Early symptoms can include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash.

Officials say people who develop symptoms should call their healthcare provider before going in person, so precautions can be taken to prevent potentially spreading measles to others.

For more information about measles, vaccination and possible measles exposure in the Philadelphia area and beyond, residents can visit the Philadelphia Department of Public Health website.

articles.title: Ingraham: Some Republicans would be ‘relieved’ to lose congressional majority
articles.summary: Fox News host Laura Ingraham said “a lot of Republicans” secretly want the party to lose its majority in November to relieve the GOP of the pressure to advance President Trump’s agenda. “I actually think there are a lot of Republicans on the Hill who will be happy not to have the burden of having…
articles.body:
Fox News host Laura Ingraham said “a lot of Republicans” secretly want the party to lose its majority in November to relieve the GOP of the pressure to advance President Trump’s agenda.

“I actually think there are a lot of Republicans on the Hill who will be happy not to have the burden of having to pass legislation,” Ingraham said Thursday on “The Ingraham Angle.” “They’re almost going to be relieved for a little while, at least, to be in the minority.”

During a discussion with Fox Business Network host Larry Kudlow on the economy and the GOP’s midterm messaging, both Ingraham and Kudlow argued that Republicans have not done enough to promote recent accomplishments that reflect positively on the Trump administration.

“One of the most incredible statistics is the Trump administration, in one year, has grown personal incomes more than Biden in four,” Ingraham said, likely referring to Census Bureau data released this week showing median household income has risen to its highest on record.

The U.S. median household income rose 2.6 percent in 2025 to $87,460, the highest level recorded since the agency began tracking the statistic in 1967.

Ingraham questioned why Republicans were not highlighting the figures more aggressively on the campaign trail.

“Why aren’t Republicans screaming this from the rooftops?” she asked.

Kudlow similarly criticized the party’s economic messaging and pointed to wages among workers in trades, including electricians, welders and pipe fitters, who he said are making “close to $200,000 a year.”

Ingraham said now is the “best time ever for men without college degrees” — a key voting bloc that has been a cornerstone of Trump’s support.

Her comments come as Republicans defend narrow congressional majorities in November amid growing voter dissent over the economy and cost of living.

Recent polling shows more voters are favoring Democrats over Republicans on issues most important to them, including healthcare, the economy and immigration, while Trump has seen record-low approval ratings linked to the deeply unpopular Iran war.

articles.body:
Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman (D) on Thursday said he feels like he has “lost to Hasan Piker,” following the popular left-wing streamer’s recent comments about the Islamic militant group al Qaeda.

“He’s an individual that just declared that we are worse than al Qaeda,” Fetterman told Fox News’s Chad Pergram. “And Democrats are campaigning with him, defending him, and my — our base loves him. So, I mean, I can’t compete with that.”

During a recent interview with Axios, Piker argued that the U.S. commits more terrorism than al Qaeda.

“Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes,” the progressive pundit said. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.”

Piker, who is one of the most popular streamers on the social media app Twitch, campaigned with Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) in the Democratic primary.

Republicans have criticized the Senate hopeful for his association with the streamer, running ads featuring Piker’s 2019 statement that “America deserved 9/11.” He later apologized for the messaging.

The GOP’s official account on the social platform X posted the clip of Piker’s latest rhetoric on Thursday, writing, “Every single Democrat who is supported by this garbage can of a human being must condemn him immediately.”

In a statement to Axios on Wednesday, El-Sayed said he disagreed with Piker’s comments, adding that he did not “give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer.”

“I am more concerned with the dangerous policies of Donald Trump and Mike Rogers that are raising the prices of gas, groceries and healthcare for Michiganders,” he said.

The Senate hopeful also noted late last month that he has “no plans” to campaign with the pundit as the midterms draw closer, and he called their association irrelevant to his Senate bid.

El-Sayed posted a slight lead over former Rep. Mike Rogers (Mich.), his Trump-backed Republican challenger, in a recent survey from The Hill/Emerson College Polling. The populist candidate held a 2-point advantage over the former GOP lawmaker in the poll.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates the race as a “toss up.”

articles.title: Cruz on Trump labeling him ‘Lyin’ Ted’: ‘The man has an instinctual genius’
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) praised President Trump’s “instinctual genius” for giving him the nickname “Lyin’ Ted” during their intense 2016 Republican presidential primary fight. In a Wednesday interview with the New York Post’s “Podcast One,” Cruz called the nickname “politically very effective” at the time, arguing Trump used it to undercut what Cruz considered one…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) praised President Trump’s “instinctual genius” for giving him the nickname “Lyin’ Ted” during their intense 2016 Republican presidential primary fight.

In a Wednesday interview with the New York Post’s “Podcast One,” Cruz called the nickname “politically very effective” at the time, arguing Trump used it to undercut what Cruz considered one of his biggest strengths with voters.

“What was so effective about it was that my single strongest attribute was that voters trusted me,” Cruz told host Miranda Devine.

“The jiu-jitsu of Trump was to take my greatest strength and make an attack that goes right at it, and I think he does that instinctually in a very effective way,” he added.

Cruz was responding to a question from Devine about how he and Trump moved beyond their contentious 2016 race.

Cruz, who won 12 states during the 2016 presidential primary, described the contest as “ugly,” but he said he believes Trump respects people who show strength.

“I don’t think he respects girly men. He doesn’t respect people who are weak,” Cruz said. “He respects people who have strength because, listen, the guy’s got a cast-iron backbone.”

Cruz later endorsed Trump in the 2016 general election, and the two eventually became political allies.

By the time Trump first took office, Cruz was joking about their former rivalry. At a 2018 Gridiron Club dinner , Cruz joked that his presidential nickname had gone from “Lyin’ Ted” to “Beautiful Ted,” after Trump began using the new moniker during Cruz’s Senate reelection campaign.

Former deputy White House press secretary Sarah Matthews criticized Cruz’s comments, accusing him of debasing himself by praising Trump despite the president’s past attacks against Cruz and his family.

“The humiliation ritual for Ted Cruz truly never ends,” Matthews, who served during Trump’s first term, said in a reaction video posted on social media. “This man is so desperate for power that he willingly debases himself like this to praise a man who quite literally called his own wife ugly and said that his own father helped to assassinate JFK.”

articles.title: Former Institute of Peace board members ask court to stop addition of Trump name to headquarters
articles.summary: Former board members for the U.S. Institute of Peace asked a federal court on Thursday to block the Trump administration from etching President Trump’s name into the facade of the institute’s headquarters in Washington, D.C. In an emergency petition filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, lawyers for the former institute…
articles.body:
Former board members for the U.S. Institute of Peace asked a federal court on Thursday to block the Trump administration from etching President Trump’s name into the facade of the institute’s headquarters in Washington, D.C.

In an emergency petition filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, lawyers for the former institute leadership alleged the administration “now intends to carve” Trump’s name into the building.

“The threatened carving would impose serious irreparable harm,” the attorneys wrote in their filing. “It is a discrete act that can and should be forestalled through a limited, status-quo-preserving modification of the stay pending appeal.”

The president’s name was already added to the building’s exterior in removable silver lettering in December. The institute’s name is carved into the facade.

The White House did not confirm or deny these alleged engraving plans when reached for comment on Friday.

“The United States Institute of Peace was once a bloated, useless entity that blew $50 million per year while delivering no peace,” spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.

“Now, the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace, which is both beautifully and aptly named after a President who ended eight wars in less than a year, will stand as a powerful reminder of what strong leadership can accomplish for global stability,” she continued. “Frivolous litigation to stymie these efforts should be rejected.”

The institute was one of the many organizations targeted for cuts by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency — an effort that sparked an ongoing legal battle.

Congress created the institute in 1984 and allocates federal funding for its programs. The institute’s headquarters building was built using a mix of private donations and federal money.

“The building — which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation — is a work of expressive architecture designed to be ‘symbolic of USIP’s’ independent ‘mission,’” the attorneys wrote in their filing.

The president has sought to affix his name to several other historic buildings and monuments around the nation’s capital.

Trump’s efforts to take over the Kennedy Center have been subjected to ongoing litigation after he fired half of the performing arts center’s board, named himself as its new chair and pushed to add his name to the side of the iconic building.

After a federal judge blocked this renaming effort on Tuesday, the president announced that the Kennedy Center would be closing “so that it can begin the process of Reconstruction.”

articles.title: Second death confirmed in Bronx Legionnaires’ disease cluster
articles.summary: As of Thursday, 13 people had tested positive for the disease and two were still in the hospital.
articles.body:
NEW YORK CITY ( WPIX ) — A second person has died in connection with the South Bronx Legionnaires’ disease cluster , according to the city’s health commissioner.

“We mourn the loss of each New Yorker, and our hearts are with their loved ones as they navigate this difficult time,” Dr. Alister Martin said on social media.

As of Thursday, 13 people had tested positive for the disease and two were still in the hospital.

Yankee Stadium is among 10 buildings the health department ordered to clean and disinfect their cooling towers.

“We are grateful to our local elected officials who have joined us in outreach efforts as we respond quickly to cut off the exposure and investigate cases. All cooling towers that tested positive through initial screening have been disinfected,” Martin added.

Health officials say it is safe to shower, drink tap water, and use air conditioners in the affected zip codes unless otherwise advised.

This latest cluster comes after 11 people died from an outbreak over the summer on Manhattan’s Upper East Side.

Legionella forms in warm, stagnant water; a cooling tower creates the perfect conditions. Health officials say older adults are at greater risk, but Legionnaires’ disease can also pose a greater threat to people who smoke or vape, those with weakened immune systems, and people with chronic health conditions including heart, lung, kidney or liver disease and diabetes.

articles.title: Senate Republican on campaigning in ‘close’ red state races: ‘These oughta be fat guy layups’
articles.summary: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said Republicans are facing unexpectedly close Senate races in traditionally red states as the party fights to maintain its majority in November. Kennedy told reporters Thursday that he plans to travel to Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa this weekend to campaign and raise money for Republican Senate candidates. “If you told me…
articles.body:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said Republicans are facing unexpectedly close Senate races in traditionally red states as the party fights to maintain its majority in November.

Kennedy told reporters Thursday that he plans to travel to Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa this weekend to campaign and raise money for Republican Senate candidates.

“If you told me six months ago I was going to be having to spend my time in those three states, I wouldn’t have believed you,” Kennedy said. “Those oughta be fat guy layups for us.”

“Now we’re going to win there,” he added. “But the races are close.”

Kennedy said Republicans need to focus their message on inflation and the economy, which have remained top concerns for voters heading into the midterms amid the Iran war.

“We’ve got to talk about the economy. We’ve got to talk about the cost of living,” he said.

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, meaning Democrats need to a net gain of four seats for control of the chamber.

The Cook Political Report rates the Senate contests in Kansas and Nebraska as “likely Republican,” while Iowa is among seven races rated as a “toss-up.”

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) is seeking a second term against Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, a pastor. Cook Political Report moved the race from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” after Hamilton won the Democratic primary in August. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since the 1930s.

In Nebraska, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) is facing independent Dan Osborn, while Iowa has an open Senate race following Sen. Joni Ernst’s (R-Iowa) decision to retire. Cook moved Iowa into its “toss-up” category last month.

Kennedy’s comments come as Republicans work to solidify their economic messaging ahead of the midterms. Recent polling shows voters are favoring Democrats over Republicans on their most important issues, including the economy, healthcare and immigration.

articles.title: Lawmakers salute staffers keeping Capitol Hill afloat: ‘Everything is grit and hard work’
articles.summary: A bipartisan group of lawmakers highlighted the integral role of staffers in the daily functions of Congress on Thursday at The Hill’s annual Notable Staffers event. Sens. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.), along with Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Bobby Scott (D-Va.), honored their staffers, who were all featured on this year’s list…
articles.body:
A bipartisan group of lawmakers highlighted the integral role of staffers in the daily functions of Congress on Thursday at The Hill’s annual Notable Staffers event .

Sens. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.), along with Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Bobby Scott (D-Va.), honored their staffers, who were all featured on this year’s list of the legislative branch’s top aides.

During the panel, moderated by The Hill’s Julia Manchester, the lawmakers said staffers work hard to achieve bipartisan success by reaching consensus between stakeholders and getting bills across the finish line.

“Everything is grit and hard work and making yourself indispensable and doing things that other people won’t do,” Booker said.

Booker added that the ideal character of a staffer isn’t someone with an “entitled” Ivy League degree, but someone who is going to work hard and distinguish themselves through their efforts.

“When you have a staffer that significant, and who goes home at night and studies to expand the knowledge that he makes available to all of us is truly amazing,” Lummis said of her staffer Chris Land, whom she touted as having an integral hand in crafting the bipartisan Clarity Act regulating the crypto industry.

Scott, who was there to honor his staffer Carrie Hughes — the health and human services director for the House Education and the Workforce Committee — said passing legislation requires speaking to different factions and growing a consensus, which relies on staffers’ good relationships on both sides of the aisle.

“You have to have people that can get along with people to put together the best coalition you can to get your legislation passed,” Scott said. “Because ultimately you can have nice legislation, but if too many people are opposing it, it won’t pass.”

Raskin — who applauded Nelly Decker, communications director for House Judiciary Committee Democrats — said the culture of a good Congress is shaped by staffers. He said members often rely on their staffers to interface with other offices on official business so they can retain their good relationship with other members.

“The people in the office really come to represent, both literally and metaphorically, the member, and they protect us a lot,” Raskin said.

Booker also highlighted that diversity among staff matters can contribute to members’ support for important bills. Booker said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) once told him that he was signing on to his bill funding sickle cell disease research because the Black members of his staff insisted. Sickle cell disease disproportionately affects Black Americans.

He noted, however, that Congress has to do more to bring in talent from all corners of America.

“Congress has got to do a lot more to pull the talent from America and present opportunities for America for people who don’t normally serve on the Hill,” Booker said. “That will make this Capitol be far better in doing its job for the American people.”
