articles.title: Hollywood handouts shouldn’t come before environmental cleanup
articles.summary: New evidence highlights the type of spending that benefits communities one can overlook when jetting from Los Angeles to Gotham.
articles.body:
Representatives from both parties are drafting a federal tax incentive for the movie industry — a move likely to give taxpayers a poor return on their money. New evidence highlights the type of spending that benefits communities one can overlook when jetting from Los Angeles to Gotham.

State and local governments have a history of throwing cash at firms to entice them to their jurisdiction. My review of credible studies regarding relocation incentives found that, on average, 93 percent of relocating firms would have come anyway. Incentives for Hollywood fit the pattern. An audit of Georgia’s Film Tax Credit found that for each dollar the state gave, 19 cents came back. Although tax revenue is just one metric, it shows the unfavorable deal taxpayers gave for Hollywood to come down to Georgia.

Governments at all levels should exit the business of ad-hoc corporate tax incentives and focus on what they are uniquely positioned to do: fund broadly enjoyed goods that others won’t. A prime example is funding the cleanup of environmental hazards that plague many communities and the restoration of the amenities they once enjoyed. A corporation can pocket a tax incentive and move on; no one can pocket a river made healthy for fish and people or a site suitable for new homes.

Abandoned mine drainage contaminates as many as 39,000 miles of streams in Appalachia alone. Interviews with residents of mine-affected areas reveal that mine-polluted waterways foster pessimism about the future and neglect in the present, with one type of pollution, mine drainage, leading to others, trash dumping. People leave such places if they have the chance: from 1990 to 2020, Pennsylvania communities with mine drainage problems and no restoration saw their population decline by 9 percent . That’s almost 1 in 10 people moving elsewhere.

Supported by public funding, grassroots organizations have built and maintained hundreds of wetland systems to treat mine drainage, improving water clarity for miles downstream. Residents near restored waterways report a new sense of pride of place and optimism about the future. As a result, longtime residents stayed and new ones came, especially those with more education.

The cost? About $240 per resident of a Census tract with restoration. By comparison, the federal Empowerment Zone program, which mainly consisted of business incentives, spent $1,500 per resident and attracted fewer people to select Census tracts.

Treating abandoned mine drainage is one of many possibilities for high-return public investments that cannot be uprooted and offshored. Brownfields are another. Remediating them — assuming no responsible party exists to do it — turns a community hazard into an asset for repurposing.

An example is Pennsylvania’s Hazardous Sites Cleanup Act program, which helped turn the site of a former steel and coke plant in Pittsburgh into innovation centers and advanced manufacturing facilities. A study of brownfield cleanups showed that by increasing property values they would generate, with reassessments, enough tax revenue in one year to more than cover cleanup costs. Compare that to the Georgia film tax credit that repays 19 cents on the dollar.

The bipartisan Ohio River Restoration Program Act , sponsored by Sens. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), aims to remediate toxic substances, protect drinking water sources, restore fish and wildlife habitat and create opportunities for public access and recreation. The act won’t produce Hollywood blockbusters, but its proposed funding is $350 million a year.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles filmmakers flying over the Ohio Valley can tap New York’s film tax credits for up to $700 million a year.

Jeremy G. Weber is professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public and International Affairs and author of “Statistics for Public Policy: A Practical Guide to Being Mostly Right” (or at Least Respectably Wrong), University of Chicago Press.

articles.title: GOP lawmakers smell something else behind Big Tech's AI doomsday warnings: 'Something else going on'
articles.summary: Capitol Hill lawmakers question whether OpenAI and Anthropic are pushing for AI regulation to stifle competition and lock in market dominance.
articles.body: Republicans on Capitol Hill are grappling over whether and how to regulate artificial intelligence companies even as top AI business leaders warn the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. The simmering debate over AI guardrails has exploded this week as House lawmakers worked through their final week in Washington until after the midterm elections. The flurry of activity was partially spurred by tech CEOs like Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman warning that the pace of innovation should be slowed after both companies saw AI models hack into other organizations of their own accord. And while some in Congress are demanding swift action, others who spoke with Fox News Digital are questioning the motivation of AI companies in calling for the government to step in. "I think there's a false sense of urgency," Rep. Troy Downing, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL Downing spent his young adulthood in tech, having previously been a research scientist at the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University and founding online calendar company WebCal, which was later acquired by Yahoo!. "Yes, we should be taking it seriously, but I think the hyperbole is misplaced right now," Downing said. "Any one of those people crying gloom and doom has the possibility of stopping it in their own shops, so there's something else going on there." Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., a former assistant U.S. attorney, also doubted AI companies' motives. AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK "I'm very skeptical of people in big business who want to leverage big government to suppress competition," Knott said. "I'm afraid that's what we're seeing. That'd be like ... Google, Yahoo, Microsoft, Apple saying, 'We need to regulate all tech.' Whether it's software or hardware. It's like, guys, you're here already, right? And if there's one thing that I'm confident in, to protect AI for good, there has to be more than one option." Still others believe lawmakers do not broadly have enough knowledge to take on AI guardrails. Rep. Jimmy Patronis, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital that Congress should instead repeal Section 230, a federal law shielding internet and tech companies from liability for what third parties post. "I think the warning is real, and I think that AI is unbelievable — look, AI is going to cure cancer. AI is going to find solutions to get rid of diseases that we never thought we could get rid of, but it does need to have some oversight. It needs a kill switch," Patronis conceded. "But again, I don't think Congress has the expertise to tell an emerging technology what's the best way to go." Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., said when asked if Congress should act before the end of this year, "It's too complex a subject. You've got to understand it." Meanwhile, President Donald Trump also joined the debate by dismissing AI companies' calls for more government regulation. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," he wrote on Truth Social. "The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" But others are pushing for the government to step in to at least some degree, with some Republicans arguing for human guardrails to ensure AI does not go too far by itself. RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS "The sooner we can act, the better," Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., chair of the House's AI task force, told reporters Wednesday. "Certainly, we've had some warning shots lately that have been very concerning ... So, God forbid we have a Chernobyl moment at some point here that really causes harm to people and focuses the public's attention on AI in a way that we hope it will never be." When asked by Fox News Digital about Trump's warning, however, he said, "I think the president was talking about the dangers of over-regulation, and that's something I very much agree with him on." RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., held a press conference alongside Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., on Thursday pushing legislation to stop "rogue" AI agents such as those that broke out of containment during trials by OpenAI and Anthropic. "We want to make sure that people remain in control. This isn't about stopping AI or stifling innovation," Lawler said. "Some states have put a moratorium on the infrastructure that powers this technology. That does not invent a kill switch." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Gottheimer said the bill "tells the National Institute of Standards and Technology [to] get in a room and set standards, so organizations can find every agent on their network, verify who built it, who's running it, watch it in real time for anything suspicious, and cut off its access the second something looks wrong."

articles.title: 25 years later, President Trump has discarded the lessons of 9/11
articles.summary: Democrats Nancy Pelosi and Bennie Thompson criticized President Donald Trump’s second-term national security policies, arguing that his actions regarding anti-terrorism funding, TSA privatization, and staffing cuts have weakened the nation’s defenses.
articles.body:
After the horrific assault on our country on Sept. 11, 2001, Congress came together to confront the failures that left our nation vulnerable and build a stronger homeland security system to prevent another attack. During his second term, President Donald Trump has dismantled and politicized our national security programs and federal law enforcement to such a degree that he is leaving us vulnerable to another large-scale terrorist attack. At the same time, he has recklessly launched an illegal and failing war in Iran — drastically increasing threats to the nation.

As leaders in Congress who have overseen — and helped create — many of our national security programs over the past 25 years, we know we need to focus on plugging real security gaps — not senselessly creating new ones while turning agencies created to protect us against the American people.

After 9/11, Congress, with bipartisan support, created anti-terrorism grants to help cities and states protect themselves from future attacks. Yet the Trump administration has wasted time and resources by making these critical grants the subject of political handwringing and litigation, while withholding, reducing or delaying hundreds of millions of dollars in security funding for our communities.

For example, the Trump administration attempted to cut New York state and New York City’s grant funding last year by $187 million and only retreated after political blowback and lawsuits — some of which are ongoing. It is an outrage that anti-terrorism grant money rightfully owed to our brave first responders, is now something communities must fight for in court.

Twenty-five years after terrorists defeated a weak aviation security system to carry out the deadliest-ever attack on U.S. soil, the Trump administration is pushing to bring back that same flawed system by moving to privatize the Transportation Security Administration — an idea straight out of Project 2025. If our aviation security is privatized, security contractors would undoubtedly carve out profits by cutting elsewhere. Going back to the pre-9/11 model would lead to weaknesses in security screening — putting traveling Americans at risk solely so corporations could make a profit.

Trump has also gone after the counterterrorism and intelligence workforces within the Department of Homeland Security, the FBI and the National Counterterrorism Center. When Democrats took control of Congress in 2007, we both worked to ensure passage of the Implementing Recommendations of the 9/11 Commission Act as one of our first acts, which, together with other reforms , mandated the integration of intelligence and bolstered information sharing across federal agencies. Trump’s purging of patriotic, career employees at these agencies has not only cost the United States deep institutional knowledge built over decades, but it has also damaged our international partnerships. Our allies are increasingly nervous about sharing information with us as Trump alienates them and cozies up to Russia.

The 9/11 Commission Report concluded that before 9/11, the U.S. government’s “most important failure was one of imagination.”

Now, with repeated warnings from the intelligence community and cybersecurity experts about China’s increased cyber capabilities and the potential cyber risks of advanced artificial intelligence, it should not be difficult for the Trump administration to imagine the growing threat of a significant cyberattack. Instead of working to prevent such an attack, Trump pushed out a third of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s staff and cut cybersecurity personnel across the federal government.

Now, with China pre-positioning on critical infrastructure networks, Iran hacking water utilities across the country, and new AI cyber risks being announced regularly, we are left with a weakened federal government that lacks the expertise and resources necessary to keep us secure in cyberspace.

Trump’s unnecessary war with Iran is making us less safe at home, too. Americans have been under a heightened threat environment since Trump picked a fight with Iran, the leading state sponsor of terrorism and a country that Trump’s National Counterterrorism Center Director said, “ posed no imminent threat .” By July, the State Department had issued a rare warning to all Americans that they could be targeted while abroad. This is in addition to Iran already attempting to attack our critical infrastructure that Americans rely on every day.

We’ve seen our adversaries engaging in more brazen behavior as they clearly want to see our country weakened. And, outrageously, they see Trump doing their work for them. They see the administration’s tunnel vision with Trump’s obsession with his mass deportation agenda. He has diverted thousands of law enforcement personnel from their normal duties , such as preventing terrorism and stopping terrorism financing, to instead carry out drastic immigration sweeps . Trump has also undone the work of the Justice Department and FBI to enforce our laws and prosecute violence. We can’t forget that our adversaries see that Trump has already let extremists who launched an attack on our democracy off the hook, pardoning over 1,500 involved in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

Instead of strengthening our efforts to stop America’s adversaries from conducting attacks on our country, President Trump is opening the door to potential new attacks by creating security gaps in almost every area of national security. With Republicans in charge of Congress unwilling — or unable — to stop Trump from weakening the nation, Democrats must be prepared to lead, hold this administration accountable for the damage it has done, and rebuild the homeland security apparatus so it protects Americans from terror threats while preserving Americans’ constitutional rights.

It is essential that our Republican colleagues wake up to the risks we face before it’s too late.

Nancy Pelosi represents the 11th District of California and is a former House Speaker. Bennie Thompson represents Mississippi’s 2nd District and is ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee.

articles.title: Supreme Court campaign ruling puts insiders and party bosses over everyday people
articles.summary: Democratic Senate nominee Roy Cooper criticized recent Supreme Court rulings that allow Republican committees to spend unlimited funds and receive discounted advertising rates during the highly competitive North Carolina election.
articles.body:
Statewide elections in North Carolina are highly competitive and extremely expensive. Voters make it the country’s ultimate swing state, having voted for President Trump and for me in 2016 and 2020. That also makes it a top target for Washington insiders and big money interests who try to buy elections for their favorite candidates.

When I announced my candidacy for Senate, we already knew big money would play an oversized role in trying to keep this seat in Republican hands. Although polls have had my campaign ahead, we always knew the race would be close. Democrats running for Senate in North Carolina often seem like they’re winning in the summer only to get their hearts broken in the fall. Our last Democratic senator was elected almost two decades ago and we have only elected two Democrats in almost 40 years.

Many people look at the polls along with the unpopular actions coming out of Washington and think we have this race won already. Instead of working to lower prices and deliver for working families like they promised, President Trump has insisted on his costly tariffs while he and his allies have dragged our country into an unpopular, chaotic and endless war, while the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and health care have all spiked.

But they just might get away with these failings because Republicans in Washington have another card up their sleeves for the midterms: their massive, multi-million dollar war chests.

Instead of doing what leaders should do and deliver results, Republicans have tossed out the rulebook and handed billionaires and special interests even more influence over our elections. This tactic upends my campaign and other close races by further silencing the voices of everyday people in favor of big money and national party committees.

It started last month with the Supreme Court’s worst campaign finance decision since Citizens United . In NRSC v. FEC , the Supreme Court removed coordination limits, giving parties and political committees, which raise money at one hundred times the limits of campaigns, the ability to spend virtually unlimited amounts of money on advertising.

This decision is uniquely painful in North Carolina. My opponent is Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee, who spent his career lobbying for Big Oil and utility companies as they raised prices and rates on families. The ruling uniquely helps candidates like him. His elite DC connections have already resulted in an onslaught of tens of millions of dollars in ads on the airwaves.

Then, in yet another emergency Supreme Court ruling — after ballots were mailed — Trump’s FCC allies completed their scheme at the Supreme Court. Upending decades of law, the court allowed the FCC to require local television broadcasters to give these same coordinated party committees a massive discount on television ads .

Now, they can not only spend unlimited amounts, but they can also do it at discount rates. The law clearly states that only candidate committees should get these rates as they are bound by much stricter campaign limits. But just like Trump’s White House Ballroom case, the court let Republicans off the hook on a technicality — not on the law.

This means the Republican National Committee, in coordination with their old boss Michael Whatley, can now buy four, five, or in some cases as many as 16 ads for the price they paid for one ad in 2024. That is a massive, legally mandated corporate-funded discount.

This is one big recipe for the wealthiest and well-connected to bail out their favored candidates. When you’re running to have the backs of everyday people, the big corporate interests tend to set their sights on defeating you.

As the former party chair running in the most competitive Senate race in the country, in one of the most expensive states to communicate, Michael Whatley is perfectly positioned to benefit from the Republican National Committee’s $130 million dollar war chest.

Life is really hard for working families right now. Everything is more expensive, from gas, to groceries to health care. I’m running to Make Stuff Cost Less. But, as Washington Republicans flood North Carolina with hundreds of millions of dollars of lies, they are banking on the fact that they can drown out that message.

I am a prisoner of hope. I truly believe our best days are ahead of us. But Washington is broken, and instead of trying to fix it, they are trying to rig the game in their favor. Enough is enough. Washington needs some North Carolina common sense.

Roy Cooper served as governor of North Carolina from 2017-2025. He is the state’s Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate.

articles.title: U.S. clears potential $24.3B F-35 sale to Saudi Arabia despite security concerns
articles.summary: The State Department just approved a potential $24.3 billion sale of advanced F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia. But some lawmakers are sounding the alarm that the deal could put America’s top military secrets within reach of China.
articles.body: The State Department has approved a potential $24.3 billion sale to Saudi Arabia for 48 F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter jet and related equipment, the agency said in a news release, as the critical U.S. ally confronts a new front in the war with Iran. Saudi Arabia has long pursued the F-35’s but to date Israel has been the only country in the Middle East to secure access to Lockheed Martin’s fighter jet considered the most lethal, stealthy and survivable aircraft in the world. “The proposed sale of this equipment and support will not alter the military balance in the region,” the State Department said in a press release. Congress was officially notified Thursday of the possible transfer of the advanced military aircraft to Saudi Arabia and some lawmakers have already raised concerns that the technology behind it could be acquired or stolen by China, which has a military partnership with the kingdom. “The Trump Administration should not move forward with its proposed sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party,” Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., said in a social media post. “Beijing has spent decades stealing American intellectual property and technology to close the gap with the United States, and we must not help them do it. We must not sell our most advanced fighter jet anywhere the CCP may be able to get its hands on the technology inside it.” On Wednesday, The New York Times cited U.S. officials as saying that intelligence analysts had raised the possibility that China could get F-35 technology by spying in Saudi Arabia or through its partnership with the kingdom. Previous arms sales to Saudi Arabia, including one for $110 billion proposed by the Trump administration during President Donald Trump’s first term, also faced scrutiny by Congress after the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, a columnist for the Washington Post. In his second term, the Trump administration prioritized weapons sales to the Kingdom as the largest recipient of U.S. arms. The approval of F-35 shipment follows Saudi Arabia’s agreement to purchase $142 billion in military equipment and services from the U.S. during Trump’s May 2025 trip to Riyadh — the largest defense sales package in history. “President Trump has made clear that Saudi Arabia is an anchor for regional security, and increased capabilities for the Saudi armed forces benefits the security of the United States and the wider region,” a State Department Spokesperson said. “The sale strengthens the U.S. defense industrial base and ensures Saudi Arabia continues to buy American.” Saudi Arabia has been fighting to turn back the advancements of the Iran backed Yemen rebel group the Houthis who have been launching drone and missile strikes into the Kingdom as they work to secure a critical shipping route in the Red Sea. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has urged Trump to take military action against the Houthis, NBC News previously reported, but so far, the U.S. has declined to join in military strikes. The State Department declined to provide a timeline for a possible shipment of the military aircraft but a spokesperson said the U.S. is committed to “further strengthening the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s capabilities to deter regional threats, protect its borders, and contribute to regional stability.” “The proposed F-35 sale reflects the strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-U.S. strategic partnership and the continued advancement of our defense cooperation,” the Saudi Embassy in Washington said in a social media post. “For decades, Saudi-U.S. security cooperation has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defense capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests.”

articles.title: Where Trump’s hunting, fishing order will have the most impact
articles.summary: President Trump signed new executive orders Thursday aimed at expanding hunting and fishing access in the U.S., rolling back restrictions on these activities. The president unveiled “Reinvigorating America’s Hunting Heritage” and “Restoring American Saltwater Angling and Recreation” during a Thursday White House Rose Garden dinner with more than 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor officials. “We…
articles.body:
President Trump signed new executive orders Thursday aimed at expanding hunting and fishing access in the U.S., rolling back restrictions on these activities.

The president unveiled “ Reinvigorating America’s Hunting Heritage ” and “ Restoring American Saltwater Angling and Recreation ” during a Thursday White House Rose Garden dinner with more than 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor officials.

“We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public, and hunters, fishers and outdoorsmen should be able to access them,” Trump said.

Here’s what you need to know about where these orders will have the most impact:

Under the hunting executive order, Trump directed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to reverse “years of overregulation” under previous administrations and expand hunting access on some federal lands.

This is an expansion upon the Trump administration’s August order , which opened up more than 92 million acres across 32 states for hunting.

The new order directs Burgum to permit hunting within 90 days of its signing in California’s Castle Mountains National Monument and within Idaho’s Craters of the Moon National Monument .

The California monument protects almost 21,000 acres of land in the Mojave Desert near Nevada. Craters of the Moon National Monument is in the south-central region of Idaho between Boise and Yellowstone National Park and features a 618 square-mile lava field.

Trump’s order allows hunting on these federal lands only for species that are not protected under 16 U.S.C. 1533 of the U.S. Endangered Species Act.

“I have determined that appropriately managed hunting would not put the objects of historic and scientific interest that these monuments protect at risk,” the president wrote in his executive order.

The president directed his administration to authorize the use of traditional lead ammunition and tackle within 180 days of the order.

Under former President Biden, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in 2023 expanded a ban on the use of lead tackle and ammunition in eight national wildlife refuges to safeguard these areas from potential lead poisoning risks.

Republican lawmakers and hunters have pushed back against these restrictions, citing increased costs associated with alternatives to lead products.

“Lead ammunition was a problem, huh? Is it better than other ammunition? I assume, huh? That’s pretty good,” Trump told the crowd at the Thursday Rose Garden event.

“I don’t know what the hell that means, but I know one thing: You wanted it,” he continued. “You wanted it, and I’m here for you.”

Promotes Sunday hunting on federal lands

The hunting order also instructs Burgum to encourage states to “promote and expand” Sunday hunting on state and federal lands within a year of its signing.

Burgum touted these new initiatives in a social media post Thursday, saying the Trump administration is committed to “putting American hunters, fishermen and outdoorsmen FIRST.”

“Sportsmen are among our greatest conservationists, and this administration is committed to supporting the men and women who help protect our public lands and wildlife,” the secretary wrote.

articles.title: 'Leftist delusions' face reckoning as one of America's biggest colleges makes major shake-up
articles.summary: UT Austin drops women's studies, gender studies and ethnic studies majors amid low enrollment and political pressure from Texas state leaders.
articles.body: Texas’ flagship public university is ending new enrollment in three majors focused on gender, sexuality and race in a move that is being hailed by many conservatives as a major victory. Students applying to the University of Texas at Austin can no longer select Women’s and Gender Studies, Mexican American and Latina/o Studies or African and African Diaspora Studies as majors, the institution has confirmed to Fox News Digital. The move follows a slew of other universities dropping similar majors and heated internal deliberations at UT Austin about whether to keep theirs. "In recognition of the changing degree offerings in the Department of Social and Cultural Analysis, the University is no longer enrolling new students in three majors: Mexican American and Latina/o Studies, African and African Diaspora Studies, and Women’s & Gender Studies," a university spokesman told Fox News Digital. "So, as you might expect, those majors have been removed from the University’s admissions applications to avoid new students enrolling in majors that are changing. Students currently enrolled in those majors will be able to complete their degree," the statement continued. LIBERAL FACULTY STILL HUGELY OUTNUMBER CONSERVATIVES IN HIGHER EDUCATION: REPORT "I don’t know the particulars of UT Austin’s programs. But this news is unsurprising. Across the Anglosphere, ethnic and sexuality studies have long been captured by political activists," Timur Kuran, a professor of economics and political science at Duke University, wrote on X. "Other state universities, and even private ones, will follow." Low enrollment has been part of the broader debate over the programs, although UT Austin has not publicly said it was the reason for ending new enrollment in the three majors. Earlier this year, the Austin American-Statesman reported that the university had just 307 students enrolled across the entirety of African and African diaspora studies, Mexican American and Latino studies, women and gender studies and American studies, citing institutional data. That represents less than 1% of the 44,315 undergraduates who were enrolled at the university in fall 2025. UT Austin, which is one of the largest universities in the nation, has also faced growing pressure from Republican state and federal officials over how it handles race, gender and other politically sensitive subjects. The University of Texas System has reviewed courses on gender identity to assess compliance with state and federal law and alignment with Board of Regents priorities. An internal email obtained by the Austin American-Statesman indicates that, while the majors may be on the way out, much of the coursework could remain. The plan appears to be to consolidate the defunct majors into a single offering. JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY "Gender and ethnic studies have transformed the study of the humanities and social sciences, and now they are what they are," Lisa Moore, the university’s chair of women and gender studies, said prior to the consolidation announcement. "We can’t unknow what we know… It’s just not the case that we can believe that only a small slice of human beings are responsible for everything that’s good about the world." Conservatives, unsurprisingly, have a less rosy view of the field. Steve McGuire, a fellow at the American Council of Trustees and Alumni, called axing the majors "the pedagogically responsible thing to do." "Excellent news. These programs are not ‘viewpoint diversity.’ They are ridiculous Leftist delusion[s] that have no place in truth-seeking institutions," J.D. Haltigan, a research fellow at the Centre for Heterodox Social Science, wrote on X. "They should be abolished entirely from every institution of higher-learning." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS Some on the right see this as a sign of things to come. "Every red state should follow suit with their universities," independent scholar Varad Mehta wrote on X. Indeed, a number of universities in red states have already scaled back similar programs. Texas A&M University, Wichita State University, the University of Iowa and the University of Toledo are among the institutions to make such cuts. articles.title: Powerful Cold War-era tool Trump could use in an AI emergency is set to expire in December
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says existing laws can rein in AI, but experts warn Cold War-era tools have never been tested against frontier models.
articles.body: One of Washington's most powerful Cold War-era tools could be used by President Donald Trump to rein in artificial intelligence (AI) if the powerful emerging technology ever becomes a national security threat. Originally enacted in 1950 to mobilize American industry during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act (DPA) has long been used to expand military production, prioritize government contracts and respond to national emergencies. Experts now say those authorities could also give the executive branch significant leverage over frontier AI companies if one of their systems posed catastrophic national security risks. Exactly how the government could use DPA's powers against a dangerous AI system remains largely untested, but national security and legal experts who spoke with Fox News Digital described a range of existing authorities that could apply — including laws in the act that encompass cyberattacks, exports, federal contracts and civil liability. THE AI REVOLUTION COULD BECOME A NATIONAL SECURITY DISASTER IF WE AREN'T CAREFUL "The authorities could be a little clearer," James Lewis, director of the Strategic Technologies Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. "But you could probably cobble together a solution using the legal authorities we have now." The question has taken on new urgency after leaders at some of the nation's most powerful AI companies issued stark warnings this week about increasingly capable models and backed calls to slow the pace of development so safety measures can catch up. Trump said this week that the administration already has "tremendous criminal and regulatory power" over AI companies as he pushed back on calls from industry leaders for new guardrails on increasingly powerful models. That largely remains because Congress recently extended most of the DPA's authorities, which were set to expire on Sept. 30, through Dec. 11, 2026. This is sure to set up another reauthorization fight later this year, right before the power of the legislative body could change after November's midterms in the new year. TRUMP PLAN TAPS US FIRMS TO FIGHT FOREIGN CYBERCRIME Lewis said the cyber threat has already changed. Finding vulnerabilities that once took months can now take days or even hours, he explained, while AI can help attackers chain smaller weaknesses together into more damaging attacks. "The threat itself is not new," Lewis said, recounting a recent conversation with a senior official from a Five Eyes intelligence partner. "We've known about this for a while, but people weren't taking it seriously." AI, he said, has "changed the landscape dramatically." The Trump administration has already begun building a framework to identify when those capabilities become dangerous. A June executive order directed federal agencies, including the NSA and CISA, to establish classified benchmarks for advanced cyber capabilities and determine when an AI system should be designated a "covered frontier model." The order also calls for a voluntary framework through which developers can give the government early access to covered models before their release — while expressly stopping short of creating mandatory federal licensing or pre-clearance for frontier AI. But knowing a dangerous capability exists is only the first problem. The next question is what Washington can actually do about it. One potentially powerful use of the Defense Production Act would come before an AI system ever caused damage: forcing companies to tell the government what they are developing. James E. Baker, a former chief judge of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces who previously served as a legal adviser to the National Security Council, pointed to the DPA's broad information-gathering authority. "What you could use the DPA for is to require reporting, and that's the first step to making sound policy," Baker told Fox News Digital. "You can have a debate about whether there should be regulation and what the regulation should look like. But you really can't argue against knowing what's happening." "That's the first place to start: know what's happening, and then you can react with either a policy prescription, a legal prescription or nothing at all." The DPA's limits, however, are just as important. Paul Rosenzweig, a lawyer and former deputy assistant secretary for policy at the Department of Homeland Security, said the law was principally designed to ensure the government could obtain goods and services needed for national defense — not to give Washington broad power to stop private companies from producing them. "The Defense Production Act is more about mandating the production of things for the United States rather than preventing the production for the general public," Rosenzweig told Fox News Digital. Where it could prove particularly useful, he agreed, is giving the government access to information. "What it does give them, I think, and this is the best part about it, is it does give them a pretty good handle for demanding more information about a defense-sensitive kind of product, which frontier AI certainly could be reasonably characterized as," Rosenzweig said. If the DPA could help Washington understand what AI companies are building, other existing authorities could potentially come into play depending on the threat. Export controls can restrict sensitive technology from reaching foreign adversaries. Government contracting rules can impose conditions on companies seeking federal business. And criminal laws continue to apply when AI is used to commit crimes. The June executive order, for example, directed the attorney general to prioritize enforcement of existing federal criminal laws against people who use AI to illegally access or damage computer systems. Trump has separately directed national security agencies to expand their use of frontier AI while requiring systems used by the military and intelligence community to remain controllable and preserve clear lines of human accountability. "I think it's important to understand that there's no broad AI exemption from generally applicable law," Rosenzweig said. Both federal and state governments already have "a host of legal authorities" potentially applicable to frontier AI, he said, ranging from tort liability and privacy rules to consumer protections and criminal law. But Rosenzweig cautioned that no one knows precisely how well that patchwork would hold up in a true AI emergency because it has never been tested. The uncertainty becomes even greater if an AI system causes damage on its own. If a model autonomously hacked a hospital, company or critical infrastructure network, for example, Rosenzweig said courts would have to determine whether the developer was negligent, whether a stricter product liability standard should apply and whether the damage could even be reliably traced back to a particular AI system. "I tend to think that liability is going to be difficult to establish early on," Rosenzweig said. "Right now, that's not where I would base my deterrence model." That uncertainty points to the limits of the government's existing toolkit. The laws already on the books give federal and state authorities multiple avenues to respond to dangerous uses of AI, but many have never been tested against a system acting with increasing autonomy. Rep. Ashley Hinson , the Iowa Republican locked in a tight Senate race, won’t be sharing the stage when Vice President Vance stumps in Council Bluffs this afternoon.

Her campaign says she had previously scheduled events. This profile in The New York Times today points to another reason why her campaign isn’t eager to shift schedule: President Trump ’s policies are not popular in the reliably red state.

Hinson notably broke with Trump over his plan to import beef from South America to lower prices, a move that will hit cattle ranchers hard. Trump’s tariffs and inflation caused by the Iran war are also making life more difficult in the rural state.

📺 Watch : Hinson’s latest campaign ad, focused on her bipartisan bona fides, gives a sense of the mood in Iowa.

Zach Lahn , the GOP nominee for governor, is planning to join Vance — underlining the different approaches Republicans are taking to the Trump conundrum. Lahn is trailing his Democratic opponent, State Auditor Rob Sand , while Hinson has a slight edge in her race, according to most polls.

Notable votes: Hinson isn’t the only Republican seeking to create some distance with the Trump administration.

Two Iowa Republicans backed an Iran war powers resolution in the House this week, breaking from their past opposition to similar resolutions.

Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn were among seven GOP members who joined Democrats in passing the resolution.

“Iowa has already paid a devastating price, including two service members killed by an Iranian drone in Kuwait. Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight,” Nunn wrote in a post on social platform X.

“I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” Miller-Meeks said in her post.

Trump is giving his initiative to lower drug prices a boost Friday, with a new effort to bring “most favored nation” pricing to some Medicaid drugs across all 50 states.

It’s the latest step in an effort that already includes TrumpRx, the Trump administration’s platform for finding discounts on certain prescriptions.

The move comes as Republicans look to make affordability a central message heading into the midterm elections. The White House says the plan could save more than $64 billion, though it hasn’t explained how it arrived at that figure.

Here’s the idea: The model would use pricing in other countries as a benchmark, with participating states getting supplemental rebates from drugmakers to bring their costs down.

The catch: Medicaid already gets significant discounts on prescription medications, leaving questions about how much additional savings the model will produce — and what it could mean for everyday prices.

The president launched TrumpRX in February and has since added hundreds of generic drugs.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday headlined a conference for Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine group he once led, telling the crowd it has a “strong and steadfast friend at the White House.”

He also explained that Trump tasked him with investigating whether childhood vaccines contribute to chronic disease — and vowed to look into “chemtrails” and electromagnetic fields.

Meanwhile, Kennedy named eight new members to a key preventive health panel, bringing specialists in areas including oncology, cardiology and gastroenterology into the mix.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ’s plan to screen troops for testosterone deficiency is back, with the Pentagon now requiring male service members older than 30 years to undergo testing.

The administration temporarily pulled its previous guidance earlier this month before issuing the new rules Thursday, which lay out a path for treatment, including hormone replacement therapy.

Hegseth framed the effort as a way to keep warfighters on the “leading edge of lethality,” while the department says it will strengthen performance and force readiness.

📰 The Hill’s Filip Timotija breaks it all down .

Senators left a closed-door briefing Thursday frustrated by what they described as a lack of clear answers on the Iran war .

The Senate Armed Services Committee convened to hear from Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby on the Trump administration’s National Defense Strategy. But Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) said the ongoing conflict with the Islamic Republic was the main focus.

The briefing also started on an unusual note, with Colby opening the floor to questions without giving an opening statement. Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) called it “very peculiar” and said there were “a lot more questions than answers.” Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) noted she was “very disappointed.”

The bipartisan frustration adds to mounting congressional exasperation over the conflict, which is nearing the seven-month mark.

Trump on Thursday said he’s facing a “big decision” on whether to “annihilate” the Iranian regime.

The teaser comes as the president is expected to meet with the leaders of six Persian Gulf nations next week on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz are also sending energy prices higher, with gas prices jumping this week. The national average hit $4.43 per gallon this week, though Trump has brushed off the surge as “a very inexpensive price to pay” to keep nuclear weapons from Tehran.

💬 The president had another chat about the Iran war with NewsNation’s Robert Sherman this morning.

articles.title: JFK’s family slams Trump over Kennedy Center: ‘How small minded, how narcissistic’
articles.summary: The family of former President Kennedy slammed President Trump for his ongoing legal battle to put his name on the Kennedy Center and to close the building for planned renovations. The Kennedy Center board, handpicked by Trump, voted Tuesday to close the main building, but Trump said the renovations will not happen as long as…
articles.body:
The family of former President Kennedy slammed President Trump for his ongoing legal battle to put his name on the Kennedy Center and to close the building for planned renovations.

The Kennedy Center board, handpicked by Trump, voted Tuesday to close the main building, but Trump said the renovations will not happen as long as the ruling blocking his name from being added to the center stands.

“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Kennedy’s niece Maria Shriver, who was the former first lady of California, said Trump’s statement “blows my mind,” calling the president “small minded” and “narcissistic.”

“That a sitting president would not let any renovations to a public building go on unless he gets to first put his name in the said building… What a sad state of affairs. What a tragedy,” she wrote on the social platform X .

“It seems that this man will not rest until his name is permanently connected to the name of a great president, whose memory this building was dedicated to,” she added.

Kennedy’s grandson Jack Schlossberg, who recently ran an unsuccessful campaign in New York’s 12th Congressional District, also weighed in.

“JFK’s legacy is unbreakable — the moon, the Civil Rights Act, Cuban Missile Crisis and the arts. Trump is a broken band in nose dive decline,” he said in a statement .

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member, sued in December to block the name change and closure plans. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled against the board and blocked its attempt to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade.

Kerry Kennedy, the daughter of former Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy, called Beatty a “national hero” for challenging the board and the administration in court.

“She has fiercely and courageously stood up for the Kennedy Center, for the arts, for Uncle Jack’s memory, for this country’s history, and most importantly, for the law, time and time again,” she wrote on social media . “We will not be bullied into silence or submission. Thank you, Rep. Beatty. We are all so grateful for your leadership.”

Kerry Kennedy’s brother, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has said in the past he has “bigger fish to fry” than worrying about a name change.

articles.title: Congress can come together to honor the Adams family
articles.summary: Four bipartisan House commissioners are calling on the Senate to pass the Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act to establish a permanent memorial for the Adams family in Washington, D.C.
articles.body:
There is plenty that Republicans and Democrats disagree about in Washington. Honoring the extraordinary contributions of the Adams family to the United States should not be one of them.

As the four members of the House of Representatives serving on the Adams Memorial Commission, we represent different parts of the country, different parties, and different political perspectives. But we are united in the belief that John Adams, Abigail Adams, John Quincy Adams, and their remarkable family deserve a permanent memorial in our nation’s capital.

Few American families have contributed as much to the founding, development and preservation of the nation.

John Adams was a leading voice for American independence, a signer of the Declaration of Independence, a diplomat who helped negotiate America’s first international alliance to secure critical financial and military support for the Revolution, and, ultimately, the second president of the United States.

His wife, Abigail, was far more than a witness to that history. During long periods when John was serving the country at home and abroad, she managed their family and farm while becoming one of his most trusted political advisers. Her remarkable correspondence provides an enduring account of the founding era, including her famous appeal to “remember the ladies” at a time when women possessed few political or legal rights.

Their son, John Quincy, carried that tradition of public service into another generation. He served as a diplomat, secretary of State, and the sixth president before returning to public service in the House of Representatives, where he became a fierce opponent of slavery.

And those three lives barely scratch the surface of the Adams family’s contributions to the United States. The family produced generations of diplomats, public servants, writers, and civic leaders whose influence extended far beyond the founding era.

Yet there is still no memorial in Washington honoring this extraordinary American family.

That omission is especially striking as Americans commemorate the 250th anniversary of our independence. John Adams helped make that independence possible. Abigail Adams helped give voice to the principles the new nation would spend generations working to fulfill. Their descendants demonstrated how the responsibilities of citizenship and public service could be passed from one generation to the next.

A memorial to the Adams family would be different from the monuments Washington already knows so well. It would not commemorate only a president, general, or individual achievement. It would tell the story of an American family — men and women, parents and children — bound together across generations by a commitment to public service. The current proposal envisions that memorial near the White House, where John and Abigail became its first residents in 1800.

At a time when Americans hear so much about what divides us, the Adams Memorial offers a small but meaningful reminder of what can still unite us. Republicans and Democrats in the House have already come together unanimously behind this effort.

The Adams family gave generations of service to the country they helped create. Two hundred and fifty years after the Declaration of Independence, it is time for our nation’s capital to give them the recognition they deserve.

The Senate should pass the Adams Memorial-Great American Heroes Act and help make that memorial a reality.

Morgan Griffith, William R. Keating, Stephen F. Lynch and John Moolenaar serve as commissioners on the Adams Memorial Commission.

articles.title: DHS' top lawyer threatens penalties for attorneys clogging asylum system
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland warned AILA against filing frivolous asylum claims, threatening penalties for immigration lawyers amid Trump's crackdown.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security fired off a warning shot to a major consortium of immigration attorneys as the Trump administration cracks down on fraudulent asylum claims while seeking to roll back the Biden administration's open-border policies. The warning letter marks an escalation in DHS' tactic of targeting illegal immigrants and problematic asylum seekers or green-card holders by also targeting the attorneys who represent them and seek to help them remain in the U.S. "Asylum offers protection to aliens who have fled their countries due to persecution by the government on account of a protected ground," James Percival warned the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) on Wednesday. TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD "To be eligible for asylum, an alien must show that he is a ‘refugee’ as defined in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A), meaning that he is unable or unwilling to return to his country because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion." Percival said asylum is discretionary and not guaranteed for someone who believes they are being targeted in their home country, even if they meet the eligibility requirements. "We have been abundantly clear: If immigration attorneys commit fraud for their clients, the attorneys will be fined," Percival told Fox News Digital on Thursday. He warned of a growing backlog of asylum cases clogging up the immigration court system and warned AILA against exacerbating it, should they then face consequences. "Filing a frivolous asylum application generally renders an alien permanently ineligible for most forms of relief and other immigration benefits ... The Department will vigorously pursue all available remedies against anyone engaging in this conduct," Percival warned in his letter. "We must restore order and accountability to our immigration framework now, or we risk dismantling the humanitarian safety net for those who need it most." In 2025, AILA previously criticized President Donald Trump after he raised concerns over "rampant fraud and meritless claims" in a directive to DHS and the DOJ. AILA officials called the missive "chilling" and rejected that their members are engaged in frivolous litigation or conduct. Fox News Digital reached out to AILA for further comment. Percival wrote Wednesday that an asylee’s persecution must be committed by a "state actor" to be considered by the U.S. system, while adding that private actions against an asylee are potentially valid when that person’s government acts in a way unwilling to confront the persecution. CHICAGO'S DEADLY JUNETEENTH WEEKEND LEAVES 7 DEAD AS TRUMP SHAMES DEM GOV FOR INACTION But he said that carve-out is a high bar, appearing to take a shot at Illinois leaders over the state's persistent crime problems. "[T]his requires an extraordinary showing, as residents of crime-ridden cities like Chicago could easily claim that the government is unwilling or unable to control private actors. To meet the high legal threshold of the government being ‘unable or unwilling’ to control the non-state actor, the alien must establish that the home government has fundamentally breached its basic duty of protection to its citizens," Percival said. DHS DIRECTS ICE ATTORNEYS TO SEEK EARLY DISMISSAL OF LEGALLY DEFICIENT ASYLUM CLAIMS With many of the border-crossers in recent years coming from Central and South America, Percival indicated that conditions in most Western Hemisphere countries are not extreme enough to warrant a legitimate basis for entry into the U.S. under current policy. "Recent trends show that individuals who illegally migrate within the Western Hemisphere generally do so not because they seek a safe haven from persecution but instead primarily due to a variety of non-humanitarian factors, including economic incentives and misinformation about migration policies," he said. He said many such meritless claims are filed to either stifle the ability for the feds to deport them or to secure grounds on which to obtain work permits. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Claims that lack a reasonable legal or factual basis and claims filed with an improper motive are improper and will be dealt with accordingly," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The warning comes as the Trump administration, more broadly, is conducting nationwide crackdowns on multiple forms of alleged fraud beyond illegitimate asylum claims, including social services fraud, election fraud and other areas.

articles.title: ICE officer pleads not guilty to lying to FBI about Minneapolis shooting
articles.summary: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer pleaded not guilty Friday to federal charges stemming from allegations that he lied to authorities about what led up to the January shooting of a Venezuelan man during Minneapolis enforcement operations. A federal grand jury indicted Christian Castro, 52, in early September on six counts of making materially…
articles.body:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer pleaded not guilty Friday to federal charges stemming from allegations that he lied to authorities about what led up to the January shooting of a Venezuelan man during Minneapolis enforcement operations.

A federal grand jury indicted Christian Castro, 52, in early September on six counts of making materially false statements to investigators. He appeared before a magistrate judge in St. Paul on Friday where he was arraigned on the charges.

Castro, who has reportedly been suspended without pay from the agency, is the first federal immigration officer to be prosecuted by the Justice Department for actions that occurred during Operation Metro Surge in the Twin Cities.

“Mr. Castro voluntarily went to Minneapolis to surrender himself, both in state court and in federal court, and he’s been released on bond, and we look forward to litigating these matters and to presenting our case in court and exonerating him,” Michael Wynn, one of his attorneys, told The Hill.

Castro is accused of lying to the FBI about how a Jan. 14 scuffle with three men, one of whom was shot in the thigh and hospitalized, unfolded.

Officials with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) initially claimed that an officer, determined to be Castro, fired a “defensive shot” after being attacked with a snow shovel and a broom handle. But court documents indicated that the men had actually dropped the items and ran toward a nearby apartment “as soon as [they] saw his pistol.”

About a month later, DHS said it was investigating what appeared to be “ untruthful statements ” made by the officer following the review of additional video evidence.

“The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct. Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated,” a former spokesperson said at the time.

Friday’s hearing caps off what has been a chaotic few weeks for Castro, who became the center of an extradition fight between Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) after Castro was jailed in Texas in late May.

Walz accused his counterpart of delay and refusal to sign the paperwork that would have authorized Castro’s transfer so he could face state assault charges in connection with the shooting. A federal judge ultimately declined to intervene, and Castro was released after 90 days.

He was arrested again Wednesday by Minnesota authorities and made his initial appearance in a state courtroom the next day.

He is required to wear a GPS ankle monitor and cannot possess any firearms as part of his bond conditions in the federal case.

articles.title: Judge isn’t swayed by government’s claims that plans for an ‘anti-weaponization fund’ are dead
articles.summary: A federal judge who blocked the creation of a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” for compensating President Donald Trump’s political allies wasn’t swayed by a government attorney’s assurances Friday that the administration has abandoned the concept.
articles.body: ALEXANDRIA, Va. — A federal judge who blocked the creation of a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” for compensating President Donald Trump’s political allies wasn’t swayed by a government attorney’s assurances Friday that the administration has abandoned the concept. U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema in Virginia didn’t rule from the bench on the government’s request for her to dismiss a lawsuit challenging the fund’s formation and operation. But the judge rejected the notion that the case’s claims are moot because the Trump administration says the fund is dead and won’t go forward. “The issues that underlie this case are still alive and kicking, in my view,” Brinkema said. The fund for compensating Trump’s political allies encountered a fierce bipartisan backlash and threatened to derail Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Senate confirmation. On Aug. 2, Blanche issued a formal order terminating the fund after negotiating for weeks with two Republican senators who wanted to see the promise in writing before they endorsed his nomination. “The case is moot,” Justice Department attorney Andrew Block told Brinkema. “The mootness has been addressed at every stage.” But the judge noted that Blanche’s assurances have been undercut by the president and other administration officials. Trump, a Republican, continued to publicly express support for the fund even as Blanche insisted it was dead. “They contradict themselves all the time,” Brinkema said. The administration created the settlement fund to resolve Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS over the leak of his tax returns. The plan stoked outrage over the notion that Trump supporters who attacked police officers while storming the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, could be eligible for payments. Attorneys from the legal advocacy group Democracy Forward sued in May, asking the Alexandria, Virginia, court to suspend the fund’s implementation temporarily and stop the Trump administration from disbursing any payouts. Plaintiffs’ attorneys argued the government can’t divert taxpayer money to a slush fund for enriching Trump’s allies. Brinkema, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Bill Clinton, agreed in June to extend an order blocking the fund until further notice from the court. Democracy Forward attorney Pooja Boisture told the judge on Friday that the administration will most likely move forward with the fund — “either in its current iteration or a new one” — if her order is lifted. The Virginia lawsuit’s plaintiffs include a fired prosecutor and a college professor acquitted of assaulting federal agents at a protest. Also named as plaintiffs are the government watchdog Common Cause; the city of New Haven, Connecticut; and the National Abortion Federation, an association of abortion providers. “This scheme is an unprecedented, unlawful, and corrupt attempt to manipulate the legal process and laws intended to prevent political interference to achieve benefits that President Trump and his political allies could not have obtained lawfully,” the plaintiffs’ attorneys wrote. Justice Department attorneys argue the plaintiffs don’t have a legal basis for claims challenging a fund that “has never existed and will not exist.” “The time has come to stop this inquisition,” they wrote.

articles.title: Obama's brother-in-law rejects civil rights, racism argument against college sports overhaul
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Murphy and the NAACP call the Protect College Sports Act a civil rights issue, saying NIL restrictions hurt Black student-athletes most.
articles.body: While a bill to add a new swath of regulations to college sports is generating a swell of bipartisan support, some opponents are suggesting that the bill itself is racist. The Protect College Sports Act, pushed by Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., has so far survived two key hurdles in the Senate and is on its way to a final vote in the coming week. However, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, the Congressional Black Caucus and Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., one of a handful of Senate Democrats pushing against the bill, have argued that the bill would disproportionately affect Black student-athletes and put their newfound agency in decision-making granted by name, image and likeness (NIL) back into the hands of White coaches and college presidents. SENATE MOVES TO REIN IN COLLEGE SPORTS 'WILD WEST' WITH SWEEPING NEW RULES FOR PLAYERS, SCHOOLS "It's a civil rights issue, that's the reason the NAACP is strongly opposing this bill, because they see it as a civil rights issue," Murphy told Fox News Digital. "I didn't make that up. That's the reality." "The athletes who will be most affected by this bill are largely Black athletes, and the people who will be helped by this bill are largely White coaches and White college sports executives," he continued. "I’m not the one who sees this as a civil rights issue, the NAACP opposes it because they see this as a civil rights issue." The Protect College Sports Act would broadly add restrictions to the transfer portal for student-athletes and create a uniform eligibility framework of five years, recruiting and tampering guardrails that establish when schools or agents can contact or recruit a student-athlete, a federal standard for NIL rules, and a revenue-sharing cap. Proponents of the bill, including former President Barack Obama's brother-in-law, Craig Robinson, who is the executive director of the National Association of Basketball Coaches, argued that the bill did not disenfranchise Black athletes. SENATE ADVANCES LANDMARK PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT, IGNORING SEC AND BIG TEN OPPOSITION WITH CLOCK TICKING "Well, you know everybody is entitled to their interpretation of what's going on," Robinson told Fox News Digital. "I would disagree with that, and I would point out that if we don't fix this system, the same student-athletes they're talking about are not going to be college educated, because you cannot get educated by transferring to four or five different schools. You can't get a college degree doing that, so that's what I would say." Robinson was one of several former coaches who made the trip to Washington, D.C., this week to promote and support the bill. Craig Bohl, executive director of the American Football Coaches Association, told Fox News Digital that the assertion that the legislation had racist undertones was "the farthest thing from the truth." CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION "You know, one of the things that has been good for me, you know, working 43 years, coaches care deeply about all our players," Bohl said. "And while I appreciate their convictions on it, it's a misguided statement." "What we're looking at is opportunities for all. We want players to have an opportunity for compensation," he continued. "We want players to be able to have the ability to transfer. We also are looking for some stability with eligibility. We don't need NFL players coming back playing in our game." The Congressional Black Caucus has argued against the bill for months and charged that its members would not support the legislation after the Supreme Court’s decision on the Voting Rights Act earlier this year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Honestly, some of those concerns initially were over redistricting, and, you know, I'm not solving that problem with this bill," Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., one of the co-leads of the bill, told Fox News Digital. "We're just trying to address the chaos that exists right now in college athletics, where 27-year-olds are playing against 17-year-olds, unlimited transfers, graduation rates are plummeting," he continued.
